messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] some stan language questions
messages.body_plain:
On 7/31/12 4:33 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, Bob.  I'm writing some stuff in BDA3 on Stan and in preparation am reading the manual.  I have some questions:
>
> 1.  Why do we need bounds in a data statement (for example, int(0,) N;)?  Data are just data, so what is the point of the bounds?   Is it for later, when we want to do "forward simulation" for posterior predictive checking and debugging?

They're optional.  There are two points.  One is to declare
the intent of the model so that it's easier to read and
understand.  Two is to catch errors as early as possible.

> 2.  In math notation, (a,b) is an open interval, i.e. it can't equal a or b.
 > In the manual, you define bounds as closed (e.g., real(0,1) takes on continuous
> values between 0 and 1 inclusive).  I have 2 questions.  (a) could we
 > use [] notation for inclusive because that would be consistent with math,
 > or is that just too messy for parsing?

Changing Stan to use () instead of [] is no problem.
It'll require changing every single model and the
doc.  The models we can probably change pretty
automatically and the doc semi-automatically.

The reason it was originally (a,b) was because it's
theoretically open.  For example, in math, exp
maps (-inf,inf) to (0,inf), both exclusive.
In IEEE arithmetic, you get underflow so that
any number less than -800 or so maps to 0 and
any number greater than 800 goes to infinity (it's
actually a value in IEEE arithmetic).

> (b) I think that for continuous models with
 > bounds, we _don't_ want the bounds to be included.

That's a bit trickier.  See above.  We'd have to
somehow bound everything away from 0 and +inf.

> Thus the notation only
 > arises for discrete random variables.  (And I agree that it would be awkward
 > to use "int(-1,2)" to indicate a 0/1 binary variable.)

Yeah, we don't want int(-1,2), int[0,1] would be better.

> I'm sure I'll have more questions to comeï¿½

Bring 'em on!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Triangle Diagnostics?
messages.body_plain:
It would be nice to add these acceptance rate vs.
parameter value histograms into the posterior analysis
parts of Stan.

There are a couple of issues:

1.  We're not currently recording proposed parameter
values that are not accepted.  Given that the same idea
works across all of HMC, NUTS and NUTS II (should that
be "NUTS Jr."?) and even Metropolis, it shouldn't be
too hard to save it.  We just need to produce some format
for it, because it shouldn't be written into the output
for real samples.

One possibility is to add it as a comment
to the CSV output the way the tuning parameter targets
are added.  Another would be to create a separate
output file with a well-defined format for sampler
analysis (as opposed to sample analysis).

2.  In general, aren't there going to be multivariate
interactions.  The high rejection space for (alpha,beta)
may not be infomrative when projected down to one
dimension.  (For example, a highly correlated bivariate
distribution with Metropolis.)

On 7/25/12 8:53 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The 0.5 was just a random value that separated the two extreme cases (good tuning and bad tuning), so I'm happy to change it.
 > But what do you mean by "the scale of the variable"?

Looking at this now, I might have been confusing the X axis
with probability of acceptance.

- Bob

Personally, I like the idea of a separate output file altogether.
That way if you switch this auxiliary output off you don't change the
format of the nominal output stats.

> 2.  In general, aren't there going to be multivariate

Yeah, it could be a problem (a more pathological example would be a 2D
triangle, i.e. a diamond).  The univariate outputs won't indicate the
poor performing regions as easily (the regions of extreme accept
probability would be smeared out) but the information would still be
useful and a clever user could reconstruct the problem area.

 >

 > I would love to make a presentation within the company and try to make a comparison with WinBugs.
 >  From the code available I've seen that there is the folder with the WinBugs examples, but after run some examples and
 > get the results, I do not know how to generate some plots within stan.
 > Do you have any code complete for make a nice comparison of Stan to WinBugs, with graphs and different times?

This is the wrong group for this discussion.
The stan-dev group is for those working on the
guts of implementing Stan.

This discussion should be on stan-users.  There's
a link on the lower lefthand corner of:

   http://code.google.com/p/stan/

We're still tweaking the language, so the manual
and syntax are about to change a little bit.

The results are currently being generated by the Stan
program in comma-separated value (CSV) notation.

What do you know how to use?  You can read CSV files
into Python, R or Matlab.  There are R interfaces to
WinBUGS (like R2WinBUGS) and to JAGS (R2jags).

For Stan, there's a very simple R wrapper that we've tested
on Mac OS X and Linux in the top-level r2stan_sys.R
file.  And we're about to release and document a much
richer and more tightly integreated interface.

Stan's strength will be in more complex models (like
ones with hierarchical covariance components) than BUGS.

You probably want to compare effective sample size
divided by time after both implementations have converged.

- Bob

> I have patched the function of computing the auto-correlations

Great news.  I hope that will be fast enough.

Any idea how much slower it is than FFTW?  (Is there
an FFTW wrapper in R?)  The reports I've seen say about
a factor of 2 or 3.

> Now it is a lot faster for 52012, which happens to be 13003 * 4 and 13003
> is a prime number.

In trying to understand why Jiqiang thought to report this,
I just took a look at the code in:

   stan/lib/eigen_3.1.0/unsupported/Eigen/src/FFT/ei_kissfft_impl.h

and there are several places where the code really wants the
input size to be factorizable into powers of 2, 3 and 5.

I also looked at the current KissFFT code, and it's changed significantly
since Eigen imported a version (in what looks to be 2009).
So, if the latest patch isn't fast enough, we can try running
the latest KissFFT for comparison.

We'd still have to pad, because it looks like it still wants
the size to be factorizable into powers of 2, 3 and 5.  (I have
no idea why -- presumably you could keep going, but it'd take
an awful lot of unfolding until we got to powers of 13003!)

- Bob

messages.subject: changed Stan interval syntax
messages.body_plain:
I changed Stan's syntax for intervals so that they match
mathematical notation (sort of -- open intervals in theory
become closed due to floating point rounding).

Variable bounds which used to look like

   BAD:  real(0,1) theta;

now look like:

   GOOD:  real[0,1] theta;

For consistency, dimension declarations for vectors/matrices
which used to look like:

   BAD:  vector(3) x[2,4];

now look like:

   GOOD:  vector[3] x[2,4];

Also for consistency, truncation, which used to look like

     BAD:   y ~ normal(0,1) T(0,);

now looks like:

     GOOD:  y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,];

I fixed the test models, but the BUGS models need to be updated,
too (I just edited out the tests for them in test/gm/parser_test.cpp).
So while the unit tests pass, the model tests will fail.

I'll fix the models and add their tests back into our unit
later tonight.  I'll also patch the manual and post a new
version on the site -- I just copy-edited it all and added
some new material (nothing about RStan yet).

- Bob

I wasn't planning on mentioning this as it's low priority, but since this change of syntax may impact it I'll at least ask.

Would it be hard to allow for vectors/matrices of bound constrained variables?  For instance, a vector or matrix of [0,1] or [0,] variables can be quite useful in multivariate timeseries models.  Right now I'm doing the transforms using unconstrained vectors/matrices and then defining transformed parameters manually.  (I know I could do real[0,1] x[4], but that ends up using a std::vector instead of an Eigen vector which impacts what can be done with the variable.)  However if we come up with a better way of handling bound constraints (eg, bouncing) the above approach no longer works.

It would be really nice to somehow allow this in the syntax and the above change in notation for vector sizes may make this hard or require another change of notation down the line if it's ever implemented.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] changed Stan interval syntax
messages.body_plain:
On 8/7/12 3:45 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

> Would it be hard to allow for vectors/matrices of bound constrained variables?

I don't think it'll be that hard to implement (maybe a couple
of days including tests).  And we definitely want to maintain
backward compatibility later for models.

And I think it's a good idea.

Right now, we allow unconstrained vector/matrix declarations

     matrix[5,4]  x;     // 5x4-matrix
     vector[4]    y;     // 4-vector
     vector[4] z[3,2];   // 3x2 array of 4-vectors

and constrained real declarations:

     real[0,]  a;         // positive real
     real[0,]  b[5,6,7];  // 5 x 6 x 7 array of positive reals

I'm not sure how to mix the syntax.  Here are some
ways we might write a 3-vector of positive values and
of values in [-1,1]:

Option 1.

    vector[0, :  3]  v;     // 3-vector of positive values
    vector[-1, 1 : 3] rho;  // 3-vector of values in [-1,1]

YUCK!

Option 2.

    vector[0,][3] v;
    vector[-1, 1][3] rho;

YUCK!  And a pain to parse because of lookahead issues.
As Marcus pointed out, there are parsing ramifications.

Option 3.

    vector[0, ](3) v;
    vector[-1, 1](3) rho;

This would be easy to code and most like what
we currently have (if I change vector and matrix
dimension declarations back to parens).

Option 4.

    vector[0, ] v[3];
    vector[-1, 1] rho[3];

Option 4 moves all vector and matrix dimensions next
to the variable, so that what now looks like:

    matrix[5,4]    x;     // 5x4-matrix
     vector[4]     y;     // 4-vector
     vector[4] z[3,2];   // 3x2 array of 4-vectors

would look like:

    matrix x[5,4];
    vector y[4];
    vector z[3,2,4];

I think it's a tossup between 3 and 4 as to which
most clearly indicates usage.  3 makes it very clear
which dimension belongs to the vector, whereas 4 shows
you the index ranges for the use of the variables.

In retrospect, we probably should've built our own
multidimensional array objects and then used an Eigen::Map
to read them as matrices or vectors where necessary.
This whole matrix vs. 2D array thing is likely to confuse
people used to something like R or BUGS.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
This syntactic issue is precisely why I mentioned it now.  If we're going to have to touch every model lets at least make sure that the syntax would allow this feature in the future.

One option (call it option 5) would be do so something C++-like:

matrix<3,4,real[0,1]> x;

This makes some measure of sense since a 3x4 matrix is a type itself which is, in this case, made up of real[0,1] variables.  A multidim vector of matrices (ie a std::vector of Eigen::Matrix) can be declared as

matrix<3,4,real[0,1]> x[5];

It could also assume that the type is always unconstrained real, making the normal syntax something like:

matrix<3,4> x;

which isn't terrible.

The one down side of this is it implies a level of flexibility that seems unlikely to be used (e.g., replacing real with something else) but I suppose that's not the worst price to pay for clarity.

Alternatively, a more palatable variation of your Option 3 might be:

matrix<3,4>[0,1] x;

I'll think on it and see if I come up with anything else...

Cheers,
Marcus

On 8/8/12 12:27 AM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Just to let you know, I got the check working for check_greater().

Awesome!  (And harder than it sounds given all
the overloading, template specialization, and compound
template parameters winging around -- I was stuck on
some nasty ordering interactions.)

For everyone else, this means we can use
Eigen vectors or row vectors in vectorized normals.
We'll have the same for other distributions as they get
vectorized.  I already have the manual description in
the vectorization section of the optimization chapter.

Here's a simple regression with improper priors:

   data {
     int[0,] N;
     vector[N] y;
     matrix[N,K] x;
   }
   parameters {
     real[0,] sigma;
     vector[K] beta;
   }
   model {
     y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);
   }

The implementation Marcus did for matrix and vector products
will also be a big win here.  We could even go further and
write a function normal_regression_log(y,x,beta,sigma) and
push one step further through the matrix-vector product.

Something tells me we're about to vectorize inv_logit :-)

> It relies on VectorView-ing either a double or vector (generic, as in
> std::vector or Eigen::Matrix). I don't see anything wrong with it, but
> do you think we'll take a performance hit on using it? If so, I can
> avoid VectorView by writing more functions.

VectorView requires a constructor call, which in turn requires
an assignment.  But it doesn't need a malloc/free.  Given
the loop bounds are known statically, they should get unrolled
along with the indexes, so there shouldn't be a cost beyond
the constructor.

We already pay the VectorView constructor price in the vectorized
normal, so if we use those instances, there shouldn't be any
additional penalty.  (This is one reason why Matt's implementation
of the vectorization was so efficient, by the way.)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I defer to the rest of you on this one.  Sometimes my instincts aren't so good on these things.  Here are my thoughts, but again I'm not the expert on designing software.  Remember the mess I made of R2winbugs…

- I agree with Bob that we should go with all parentheses or all brackets.  Mixing parens and brackets is a recipe for disaster.  I think it's ok to go either way.  I don't even feel so stronly about closed vs open brackets, although as you know from my earlier conversation I liked the closed brackets for discrete integer variables that go from 0 to 1 or from -1 to 1 or from 1 to 10 or whatever.

For similar reasons, I worry that angle brackets will be confusing.  Again, one more thing for the user to remember:  "use square brackets everywhere, except for bounds where you need angle brackets."  I prefer the R-style convention of indicating arguments via names rather than punctuation.

- Possibly because of my Fortran backrgound, I'm not thrilled with the "matrix" type.  My inclination is to have scalars and arrays, which can be 1-way, 2-way, 3-way, etc.  I recognize that certain functions will work in certain ways with 1-way and 2-way arrays (inner product, outer product, matrix multiply, transpose, matrix "solve", probably some other things), but I assume the parser can figure that out since everything is declared anyway.

- Thus, I prefer something like this:
real[3,4] x;
or
real[3,4][floor=0,ceiling=1] x;
or
real[3,4][bounds=[0,]] x;
or
something clever that someone comes up with,

rather than

matrix[3,4] x;
or

matrix<real[0,1]>[3,4] x;

etc.

To me, it just sems redundant to label variables as scalar or vector or matrix or array.  I like the parallelism of:
real x;
real[3] x;
real[3,4] x;
real[3,10,4] x;
etc.

I do recognize that then this makes it trickier to add bounds, but I think that's ok.  Bounds are special and I don't mind using somewhat of a clunky notation for them.

See you
A

On 8/8/12 3:29 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> B
> As I sent in my last email msg to the group,

Could you resend -- I think I missed it.

> I'm not so thrilled with notation such as real, vector, matrix (I assume we're using "array"
 > for arrays of more than 2 dimension?).  I'd prefer if we could just use "real" for
 > real, "integer" for integer, etc.  Perhaps we can discuss, this isn't something
 > that is necessary perhaps, I'd be interested in hearing the rationale for doing it the way
 > you're doing it now.

The rationale for "int" vs. "integer" is that it's
conventional in every programming language.  You
already had us change "double" to "real" and it's no
problem to change "int" to "integer".

NOW is the time to do it.  I will not want to change
these kinds of superficial details after our first stable
release because it'd require our users to change all their
models.

There are full details of variable types and their
declarations in the variable declaration
chapter of the doc.  Could you maybe take a look through
the doc and send us other comments you have about syntax?

Here's some examples of what things look like now
for simple integer, real, and array declarations:

   real a;           // unconstrained real
   int b;            // unconstrained integer

   real c[5];        // 5-array of reals
   real d[5,6];      // 5 x 6-array of reals

   int e[3,4,5];     //  3 x 4 x 5 array of integers

Vectors and matrices have the following syntax:

   vector[5] f;      // 5-vector (of reals)
   row_vector[4] g;  // 4-row-vector (of reals)
   matrix[2,3] h;    // 2 x 3-vector (of reals)

In particular, note that a 2x3 matrix is NOT the same
thing as a 2x3 array.  This distinction is built in at
a fundamental level.

The basic data types are:

   int            (with optional range constraints)
   real           (with optional range constraints)
   vector         (require # of rows)
     simplex      (require # of rows)
     ordered      (require # of rows)
   row_vector     (require # of cols)
   matrix         (require # of rows and cols)
     corr_matrix  (require # of rows/cols)
     cov_matrix   (require # of rows/cols)

The indentation is on purpose -- simplex and ordered types are
implemented as vector types and corr_matrix and cov_matrix types
are instances of matrix.  So you can assign a vector to a simplex
or ordered type, but the constraint will be enforced at the end
of the block in which the variable is declared.

Arrays of any dimensionality can be made out of any of
the basic types.  So, for instance,

    simplex[4] theta[10,5];

declares theta to be a 10 x 5 array of 4-simplexes.
theta[7] is a 5-array of 4-simplexes, theta[7,2] is
a 4-simplex, and theta[7,2,1] is a real value between
0 and 1 (inclusive).

The reason we need to declare the constraints on parameters
is that we need to do the transforms.  The reasons there
are constraints elsewhere is for error checking.

- Bob

or
matrix[bounds=[0,1]] x[3,4,5];
or

> or

There aren't any angle brackets yet -- we're just making
sure that the current language is extendable to something
reasonable.

We could start naming arguments.  The only issue is verbosity.
So we could also have an order-only usage like in R.

A bigger issue is moving the matrix sizes into
the array declaration.  What we have now is:

   matrix[4,5] x[3];

for a 3-array of 4x5 matrices to

   matrix x[3,4,5]

This is possible, but I worry that it won't be clear where
the matrix is.  An alternative would be to put the named arguments
on matrix:

   matrix[rows=4, cols=5] x[3];

or

   matrix<rows=4, cols=5> x[3];

The angle brackets are traditional in C++ and Java for type
modifiers.  Using separate notation for different
things is easier to read, if not easier to remember.  (Brackets
are very ugly typographically for some reason I don't understand.)

    simplex[5] theta[3,4];

for a 3x4 array of 5-simplexes, we could write:

    matrix[simplex,rows=5] theta[3,4];

or

and infer the number of columns matches the number of rows?

messages.body_plain:
I think ideally it would be good to do something more like you're expecting from Fortran but right now we don't have a general multidimensional array object which can map efficiently onto an Eigen::Matrix object.  The practical side of that is the following:

real theta1[8]; // theta1 is an array

and

vector[8] theta2; // theta2 is a vector

results in objects of two different types which are handled differently.  For instance, you can't write

real A[8,8];
b = A * theta1;

but you can write

matrix[8,8] A;
b = A * theta2;

This is the matrix-vs-array distinction that Bob mentioned in the previous email.

Basically, if you want to do linear algebra, you have to use a vector or a matrix type.  If you don't care about that and are only accessing elements directly then you can use vector, matrix or an array.

If at some point in the future we implement a multidimensional array object which can interface with Eigen::Matrix, then the vector and matrix types can become aliases to the array class and declaring bounds on elements becomes consistent across the board.  This is part of why I was thinking of using matrix<real[0,1]> because eventually this notation would no longer be needed so there's no point making the real[0,1] case ugly.

Also, the angle brackets are for declaring a type on a matrix, the bound would still be with square brackets.  In other words: use square brackets for applying bounds to variables, and use angle brackets to declare the element type of a matrix.  Also note that this latter case (the angle brackets) would only be necessary if someone wanted to include a bound on the elements of the matrix.

Cheers,
Marcus

and be done with it :)

> On Wed, Aug 8, 2012 at 5:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:

I'm not saying it's impossible, but I don't see how
we could make it work.  It would require a richer
type-inference scheme than what we have, which only
casts an int up to a real.  Given the way code's generated,
it'd be easiest if we could do it on the C++ side.
But there are several issues (see below).

Overall, though, I prefer stricter typing with less
coercion.  I think it makes the programs easier to understand
and debug.

What we've done in the probability functions is make
a vector view wrapper so that we can treat a scalar
the same way as a vector.  But if we started allowing

>     A bigger issue is moving the matrix sizes into
>     the array declaration.  What we have now is:
>
>        matrix[4,5] x[3];
>
>     for a 3-array of 4x5 matrices to

>        matrix x[3,4,5]
>
>     This is possible, but I worry that it won't be clear where
>     the matrix is.
>
>
> I would strongly argue against this.  I think it would be confusing and lead to a lot of problems.  For instance, with
> the above, x[1,:,:] would be a 4x5 matrix but what would x[:,:,1] be?

Right now, x[1] is well formed, but neither x[1,,] nor x[1,:,:] nor x[:,:,1] is.
I started going down that route.  It would involve either more views or
copying.  Either way, it would be nice to support.

 > If it's a 3x4 matrix, then it would involve a lot
> of unpleasant copying.  So long as internally a matrix has to be 2D, that should be explicit to users, like it is now.

That's my preference, too.

> In a world with more hours in the day I would go and implement a multidimensional array with a Map for Eigen::Matrix to
> allow us to just do:
>
> real x[3,4];
>
> instead of
>
> matrix[3,4] x;
>
> or
>
> real[0,1] x[7,8];
>
> and be done with it :)

This isn't quite going to yield the same result because
it doesn't distinguish row vectors from column vectors.
The problem I see is with declarations

    real x[5];
    real y[5];

the expression (x * y) is ambiguous.   If x is a row
vector and y a column vector, then (x * y) is a scalar.
If x is a column vector and y a row vector, then
(x * y) is a matrix.  Or maybe we'd only promote 1D arrays
to column vectors?  Then (x * y) would be undefined, but
(x' * y) and (x * y') would be well-defined.

And this isn't just a type issue of distinguishing a 1x1
matrix from a scalar -- there are different result shapes!

At the underlying storage level it would make sense
to do our own implementation rather than using std::vector.
It'd be faster and less bulky.

Then we could use as_matrix(x), as_vector(x), or
as_row_vector(x) to create a matrix view of the underlying
data wherever necessary.  I don't know how hard it would be
to implement a new Eigen-like matrix wrapper (I haven't studied
how Map is implemented -- looking into Eigen always makes my
head spin).

In Stan, we could also just do the copying.  So we could have:

    real[,] to_array(matrix);
    real[] to_array(vector);
    real[] to_array(row_vector);

    matrix to_matrix(real[,]);
    vector to_vector(real[]);
    row_vector to_row_vector(real[]);

With the way we're using Eigen on an operation-by-operation basis
(I know, Ben, this isn't optimal!), this might not make that
much of a difference performance-wise.

> At any rate, since this is all started based on a feature that's not yet implemented (vectors and matrices of bounded
> variables) and is not likely to be widely used at first I think we can let it rest for the near term.  There are options
> which are consistent with the current notation (matrix<real[0,1]>[3,4] for instance) and don't cause parsing problems.
> And, since it relates to the larger issue of multidimensional arrays, it may get solved in another way at some point in
> the future.

We just need to nail down what the basic syntax is.
I guess we've found our bike-shed issue

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_Law_of_Triviality

But then getting basic syntax right is important for
understandability of the code.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
B
See comments below.
A

On Aug 8, 2012, at 11:11 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> The main reason for having these types is that we can
> infer that for
>
>    row_vector * vector
>
> the result type is real.

If you think that's a good idea, we can go with it.  My inclination (based on my background from R) is to _not_ allow just plain "*" to do this.  I would prefer something more explicitly such as
inner (a, b);
which would return the inner product of a and b whether or not they are both row_vectors, both vectors, or one of each (in either order).  Actually, I would prefer to just have "vector" and forget about "row_vector" but I could see (perhaps) how row_vector will help when we're doing matrix multiplication.

I'm not saying to go change everything right now; it just seems like it might be worth discussing.  My worry about "*" is the potential confusion, I see the code as less readable because when I see "*" I will have to go back to declarations to see what is what.  "inner(,)" seems more clear to me.

>
> Do you think we'll have cause to use matrix operations on
> integer-based matrices?

Possibly.  This comes up in some models in psychometrics (and, I assume, in CS) with latent classes.  Then again, we don't know how we will be fitting such models, as HMC doesn't work there!

> There aren't any angle brackets yet -- we're just making
> sure that the current language is extendable to something
> reasonable.

I thought you were proposing angle brackets for constrained parameters.

> We could start naming arguments.  The only issue is verbosity.
> So we could also have an order-only usage like in R.
>
> A bigger issue is moving the matrix sizes into
> the array declaration.  What we have now is:
>
>  matrix[4,5] x[3];
>
> for a 3-array of 4x5 matrices to
>
>  matrix x[3,4,5]

No, I am going back to your original plan.  I think "matrix[4,5] x[3]" is fine!  That was the point of my past email ("wow, cool!"):  now I understand the maotivation for "matrix[4,5] x[3]" and I love it!  Actually, I could imagine uses for "array[4,5,6] x[7,8]" but maybe we can wait on that…

What I'm getting at is, your notation "vector" and "matrix" has two distinct advantages. First is your motivation of computational efficiency:  vector and matrix types allow you to implement fast vector computations.  Second is for statistical notation.  For instance, imagine a hierarchical model in which each person has a vector of parameters theta of length 4, and there are 40 people.  Then you could do "vector[4] theta[40]".

It's the Pinnochio principle all over again:  your comptuational idea, when implemented, suggested a statistical idea.

Now that I'm thinking about it, there are other ways of implementing the statistical idea.  For example, suppose in my example we simply defined "real theta[40,4]" but then we wanted to give names to the rows or columns of theta.  We could use a notation such as "theta_1" for the rows (thus theta_1 is a set of 40 vectors, each of length 4) and "theta_2" for the columns.  This would generalize, for example if we have "real x[3,4,5]", then x_13 is a set of 4 matrices, each of dimension 3x5.

I could see how this general notation could be useful at some point but it doesn't seem worth worrying about now.

>
> This is possible, but I worry that it won't be clear where
> the matrix is.  An alternative would be to put the named arguments
> on matrix:
>
>  matrix[rows=4, cols=5] x[3];
>
> or
>
>  matrix<rows=4, cols=5> x[3];

No, I _don't_ think that will be needed.  It seems clear enough in "matrix[4,5] x[3]" that 4 and 5 are the dimensions of the matrix.

The only place where I wanted names was for bounds.

>
> If we do go with names, I'd prefer "lb" and "ub" to
> "floor" and "ceiling", because the latter have integer-rounding
> interpretations.  So that'd give us something like:
>
>   real[lb = -1, ub = 1] x[12,7];
>
> for a 12x7 array of reasl bounded in [-1,1].  Then we'd be
> able to write
>
>   real[-1,1] x[12,7];

That could work, or instead of "lb" and "ub" (which to me seem too cute and unix-like, in the mode of "cat"), we could use "bounds", hence "real[bounds=[-1,1]] x" or even "real[bounds=-1,1] x" etc.

>
> as we do now.  It'd also open the way for us to write:
>
>   real[lb = -1] x[12,7];
>
> instead of
>
>   real[-1,] x[12,7];
>
> And then maybe instead of writing:
>
>   simplex[5] theta[3,4];
>
> for a 3x4 array of 5-simplexes, we could write:
>
>   matrix[simplex,rows=5] theta[3,4];
>
> or
>
>  matrix[constraint=simplex, rows=5] theta[3,4];
>
> and infer the number of columns matches the number of rows?
>

Shortcuts are fine but unambiguity is better, I think.  The real issue, though, is that once we're fitting big models (e.g., the 12 predictors with all the 2-way interactions), I think we'll want some way for the user (i.e., me) to set up shortcuts, or subroutines, or macros, or whatever.  The important gains will not be from removing keystrokes or characters within a line, the important gains will come from chunking in some way.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] bounds + rows/columns syntax decision
messages.body_plain:
I prefer named bounds but not named rows and columns.  Thus, for example:

int[bounds=0,] c
int[bounds=0,1] d
real[bounds=-1,1] f[4,5]
matrix[bounds=-1,1][4,5] m

Another reason I don't like the "rows" and "columns" thing is what happened to R:  different functions use "row", "rows", "nrow", "nrows", "col.means", "colnames", etc (and I'm probably getting some of these wrong).  Sometimes column is "column" (parallel to the word "row") and sometimes it's "col" (parallel to the three-letter word "row").  Yuck!  If we never use the words "row" or "column" at all, I'll be happy.

As a non-C-user, I'd go with square brackets everywhere so that users don't have to try to remember when they need angle brackets.  But if you think that's silly, we can go with the angle brackets!

> -------------------------

> The only issue I see with what we have now is the

>
> vs. what we have w/o names:
>
>  vector[3] v;
>  row_vector[3] rv;
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Our error checking is now vectorized!

Now that I've gotten it done, I think we can do it with half the code,
at the cost of leaning on VectorView. Right now, I've got two
implementations of each check: one for a vector, another for a scalar
(double or agrad).

On Wed, Aug 8, 2012 at 1:38 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> VectorView requires a constructor call, which in turn requires
> an assignment.  But it doesn't need a malloc/free.  Given
> the loop bounds are known statically, they should get unrolled
> along with the indexes, so there shouldn't be a cost beyond
> the constructor.
>
> We already pay the VectorView constructor price in the vectorized
> normal, so if we use those instances, there shouldn't be any
> additional penalty.  (This is one reason why Matt's implementation
> of the vectorization was so efficient, by the way.)

That makes sense. Is getting hit with a constructor for each check an
issue? Alternatively, we could pass in the VectorView, but I think
that would end up making the error message a little less clear with
our current implementation.

Hi all.  Now that Stan works, I can see some new issues.  Just for laffs I ran the 8-schaools with n.iter=100.  Here's what we got:

tau       9.462  6.327   2.569 5.198  8.281 12.017 21.786  47.363 1.046

For each parameters, ESS is a crude measure of effective samples size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).

Then I tried it again:

4 chains: each with n.iter=100; n.warmup=50; n.thin=1; 100 samples saved.

           Mean    SD   2.5%   25%    50%    75%  97.5%     ESS  Rhat

theta[1] 10.543 6.960 -0.959 5.872 10.231 14.435 26.046  34.411 1.120
theta[2]  8.236 5.873 -2.728 4.397  8.527 11.917 18.902 101.412 1.008
theta[3]  6.910 6.554 -5.845 2.141  7.595 10.565 20.521  46.186 1.084

theta[7] 10.823 5.186  2.402 7.682  9.968 13.406 21.518  40.083 1.072
theta[8]  8.030 6.633 -6.384 3.071  8.908 11.706 19.859  80.245 1.000
mu        8.412 4.494  0.210 5.082  8.649 10.785 17.620  29.995 1.086
tau       5.652 3.357  1.445 3.178  4.586  8.037 13.208   6.211 1.289

Here are some problems:
1.  In the note at the bottom, "samples" should be "sample"
2.  I'd like the default output to be 1 digit after the decimal place, not 3 (e.g., "10.5" rather than "10.543") and we should round ESS to 0 decimal places.
3.  More worryingly, check out the first simulation above.  R.hat < 1.1 (rounded) for all parameters and is less than 1.05 for tau.  Yet the inference for tau is all wrong, the posterior mean is 9.5 rather than 7.2 (the result we get after running for 10000 iterations).  Doing a quick calculation based on ESS:  the mean should be estimated at an accuracy of sd/sqrt(n.eff), that would be 6.3/sqrt(47)=0.9.  So the result is over 2 se's from the true value.  Maybe this is ok, it's just bad luck?  Perhaps the message is that, despite what David Mackay says, an ESS of 12 is not enough!
Are we using our current preferred ESS formula here?
4.  Given point 3 above, I'm thinking that our output should include, right next to the mean, the se of the mean (calculated as above).

Now the good news:  Stan is amazingly fast.  I ran it for 100,000 iterations and, once compiling was done, it took aboout 15 seconds for all 4 chains together!

Compile time is still a bit slow (at least compared to runtime for a simple model).  Here are 2 questions:
1.  After compiling a model, can stan save the object code so that it doesn't need to recompile when we run it again?  I ask because in practice I'm always running models over and over and over.
2.  Even better, could stan automatically search the appropriate directory for the object code and then automatically just use the already-compiled model if it exists?  That would be a huge help in practice.

Finally, one more thing that's interesting, regarding ESS.  Here are some values of n.iter and ESS for tau (from second halves of 4 chains):

n.iter  ESS
1000  55
10000  450
100000  990

Huh?  Shouldn't that last number be about 5000?  I tried the three again and got the folloing:

n.iter  ESS
1000  86
10000  430
100000  850

What up?

Hi.  I just ran 8-schools for a million iterations (4 chains, it took about 2 or 3 minutes!). stan(model.code = , data = , ...)
stan(model.code = , data = , ...)

I think we need some cache mechanism to make it possible to compile the code once if model.code (or file) is the same for another call.  This is doable, it is a bit like http://ccache.samba.org/ then.

fit <- stan(model.code = , data = ,....)
fit2 <- stan(fit, .....)

As I am not using mcmc::chains, actually I could use any parallel approaches based on multiple processes R has such as multicore (http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/multicore/index.html), but even multicore may not work on all platforms.  I am not sure how easy it is to make it just an option.

I'm using Stan for research!

1.  For some reason the page numbers are sporadic, for example no page numbers between 60 and 70.  (I actually noticed this because I was actually looking for a particular page, having used the table of contents.)

2.  It would help to have a single pdf document with the Jags examples with Jags and Stan code.  I could then use this as a template.  As is, I'm doing a lot of guessing, trying to figure out what will work and what won't, with syntax.

3.  Can we put multiple data or parameter declarations in a single command line?  I tried the following but it did not work:

    int[0,] J.1, J.2, J.3; // number of persons, between-plot treatments, within-plot treatments

I switched to the following which was fine:

    int[0,] J.1; int[0,] J.2; int[0,] J.3; // number of persons, between-plot treatments, within-plot treatments

But the first form above would obv be convenient if it is possible.

4.  I have a vector variable, real theta.1[J.1], and I give it a prior all at once:

    theta.1 ~ normal (0, s.1);

That seems to work.  But I also have a two-way array, real theta.1.3[J.1,J.3], and when I try to give it a prior all at once, it fails:

    theta.1.3 ~ normal (0, s.1.3);

Could it work to allow such a call?  It would be convenient for hierarchical models.

5.  I had the following line:

    for (i in 1:n)
       y[i] ~ normal (mu + theta.1[i.1[i]] + theta.2[i.2[i]] + theta.3[i.3[i]] + theta.1.3[i.1[i],i.3[i]] + theta.2.3[i.2[i],i.3[i]], s.error);

Would it be possible to write this R-style with the looping implicit, like this?

       y ~ normal (mu + theta.1[i.1] + theta.2[i.2] + theta.3[i.3] + theta.1.3[i.1,i.3] + theta.2.3[i.2,i.3], s.error);

If not, that's fine, I'm not saying that Stan needs every possible feature.  I'm just curious.

Right now I'm still getting compilation errors, am working on debugging my model...

A

- Instructions for setting up Stan

- Stan manual
- Bugs examples
- Stan mailing lists

messages.body_plain:
This is related to C/C++'s prohibition on . in variable names.  It could be worked around, but would be tedious.  Underscores are viable though if you want to use those instead.

In summary (this should be in the manual somewhere and maybe checked in the parser) variable names:
 - Must consist of only letters, numbers and underscores.
 - Cannot begin with a number.

Cheers,
Marcus

On 8/10/12 6:27 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I'm using Stan for research!
>
> 1.  For some reason the page numbers are sporadic, for example no page numbers between 60 and 70.  (I actually noticed this because I was actually looking for a particular page, having used the table of contents.)
>
> 2.  It would help to have a single pdf document with the Jags examples with Jags and Stan code.  I could then use this as a template.  As is, I'm doing a lot of guessing, trying to figure out what will work and what won't, with syntax.

You should at least glance through the manual.

But I understand that most users won't, so this is a good
idea.  I'd rather NOT include the JAGS examples, as I think
it'll be confusing for people scanning.

I would have written a simple BUGS/JAGS to Stan conversion
guide, but it's rather complicated.

> 3.  Can we put multiple data or parameter declarations in a single command line?  I tried the following but it did not work:
>
>      int[0,] J.1, J.2, J.3; // number of persons, between-plot treatments, within-plot treatments

It's on my to-do list, so you'll get lists like this
in the future.  That, and I want to be able to allow

     int J <- 10;

as well in blocks that allow variable definitions (all but
data and parameters).

You can't have "J.1" as a variable name -- no periods, only
underscores.   As usual, I followed the usual (i.e., C++, Java,
etc. approach to variable names), not BUGS/R.

> I switched to the following which was fine:
>
>      int[0,] J.1; int[0,] J.2; int[0,] J.3; // number of persons, between-plot treatments, within-plot treatments
>
> But the first form above would obv be convenient if it is possible.
>
> 4.  I have a vector variable, real theta.1[J.1], and I give it a prior all at once:
>
>      theta.1 ~ normal (0, s.1);
>
> That seems to work.  But I also have a two-way array, real theta.1.3[J.1,J.3], and when I try to give it a prior all at once, it fails:
>
>      theta.1.3 ~ normal (0, s.1.3);
>
> Could it work to allow such a call?  It would be convenient for hierarchical models.

It's possible, but a bit of pain.  We have to generalize
the vectorization, which in this case, requires a real
calculation to deal with arbitrary arrays.

Then we need to decide how it'll work.  Is it OK to
allow

     theta ~ normal(mu,sigma)

if theta is a 4x3-array, mu is a 2x6-vector and
sigma is a 12-vector?  What about mixing a 4x3 array
and a 4x3 matrix?

If the shapes have to match, it's going to be significantly
harder to allow arrays.

Error checking would need a lot of work, as would the
vector wrappers.

> 5.  I had the following line:
>
>      for (i in 1:n)
>         y[i] ~ normal (mu + theta.1[i.1[i]] + theta.2[i.2[i]] + theta.3[i.3[i]] + theta.1.3[i.1[i],i.3[i]] + theta.2.3[i.2[i],i.3[i]], s.error);
>
> Would it be possible to write this R-style with the looping implicit, like this?
>
>         y ~ normal (mu + theta.1[i.1] + theta.2[i.2] + theta.3[i.3] + theta.1.3[i.1,i.3] + theta.2.3[i.2,i.3], s.error);
>
> If not, that's fine, I'm not saying that Stan needs every possible feature.  I'm just curious.

I had to fire up R to see what its behavior is here.

   > a = c(1,2,3)
   > a[c(2,1,1,1)]
   [1] 2 1 1 1

If v is a vector and s is a scalar, we already have
(v + s) doing the right thing in treating s like
a vector with duplication.

So the feature we need is just to have an array, vector or
matrix with an index consisting of an int array to return
a vector.

This is the easiest to implement of the requests :-)

>
> Right now I'm still getting compilation errors, am working on debugging my model...
>
> A
>
> P.S.  Stan's parser errors are awesome.

There aren't any tests on the messages themselves, so let
me know (with model source) if you find an error message
you can't understand.

- Bob

The error message here is tricky because variables
get used in contexts that could also be a function
name or number or bracket.

model {
   STATEMENT
   ...
}

where STATEMENT can be

  a_1 ~ foo();
  4.2 ~ foo();
  (a + b) ~ foo();
  {  a ~ foo(); }

So we cna have any of a variable (a_1), a numeric literal (4.2),
a complex expression ((a + b)), or a block ({ ... }).   It can
also be just a close curly brace ('}') to end the block.

If I've seen an open brace ('{'), then I have to get a
statement of some kind or a close brace -- I doubt the error
message is that clear, nor do I know offhand how to make it
that clear (I'll think about it some more).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan hangs with empty model
messages.body_plain:
It's hanging during find_reasonable_parameters(), which looks for the
smallest step size that results in poor accuracy and then dials that
back. The problem is that for this empty model *any* step size will
result in perfect accuracy. So it never quits.

I've pushed a change that should address this problem—it checks for
huge or zero step sizes during find_reasonable_parameters() and throws
std::runtime_errors with the message "Posterior is improper. Please
check your model." if the step size goes above 1e300 or "No acceptably
small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not
continuous?" if the step size goes to 0.

Feel free to change the wording.

Matt

PS: We don't have to do guesswork to figure out where the program is
hanging—a quick profiler run was all it took to isolate the problem.

For a long time, there was no S4 print function, and that might still be the case today. Instead, the S4 function that prints to the screen is show() and you can write methods for that. If someone does

posterior <- stan()
posterior

This will implicitly call the show() method, but would implicitly call the print() method if posterior were not a S4 object.

> CRAN.  CRAN says the boost package is 404 since boost-1.0.0
> in 2004:

Mav and I had discussed this on the list. The boost R package is abandoned, but the CRAN servers have some version of Boost on them. Presumably, this is the version of Boost in the Debian testing repository, which is 1.49. Thus, if the version of Boost that CRAN has is sufficient to build stanc (and thus RStan), it is possible to require that a particular version of Boost be available on the system to compile the models.

Conceivably, we could do the same thing with Eigen. Depend on RcppEigen so that the CRAN servers can build RStan but require a particular version of the Eigen headers be available on the system to compile the models.

That is always available as a fallback plan, although it seems confusing to users. There is no law that says we can't also host a giant version of RStan on GoogleCode that has all of Boost and Eigen in rstan/inst/include for people who are unable to follow instructions for how to install Boost and / or Eigen themselves.

I don't know that much about Boost, but I still think it is feasible for (R)Stan to support whatever version of Eigen RcppEigen has at the moment and whatever is the latest stable Eigen on the Eigen website. Most of the time, they won't diverge that much, and if there is something in (R)Stan that works with one but not the other, then we would want to know about it because it is probably a regression.

Ben

Hi, Bob.

1.  mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> is good for me.

2.  Here's what I would put on the home page:
a.  One or two-sentence description of Stan along with the logo
b.  Status indication of latest version (e.g., "Latest versions:  Stan1.03 released 9 Aug 2012, Rstan 1.1 released 10 Aug 2012")

g.  For more:  link to googlecode page
h.  How to join the user group [with a note that info on the developer group is on the googlecode page]

We don't need to link to C++ API, that can be on the googlecode page.  We don't need to link to the licence info, that can be on the googlecode page.  Etc.

I am happy to have the google code page be as crowded as you'd like.  But I'd like the homepage to be clean.  Users like me would liek the manual, the installation instructions, the examples, and to see whether anything is new.  More sophisticated people can go to the googlecode page.  Thus, I'm not suggesting to remove any info, I just want to create a clean friendly portal.  Right now, I'm in the stan project but I had difficulty finding what I need.

mu is a vector when there's an underlying
regression.

Thinking about using matrices by flattening
them to vectors (and thus allowing an easy
extension of the VectorView we have), we
immediately run into order issues.

Eigen will flatten a 2x3 matrix using column-major
order:

   (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), (2,2), (1,3), (2,3)

and a 2 x 3 matrix in C++'s row-major order would be

   (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,2), (2,3)

This will confuse people if we do it and make the
code slow for one of Eigen or std::vector if we don't.

Let me think about this some more.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan float
messages.body_plain:
Interesting.  But complex from an implementation point
of view because we want to interrupt a loop within Stan,
but don't want to have to depend on R to do it.

So we'll have to provide a plug-in callback interrupter.
Shouldn't be too hard.

We could add a template parameter IF for the type of interrupter
to all the sampler classes, then down in the guts of
loops, have something like:

   template <class IF, ...>
   class XXX_sampler {

     IF& interrupter_;

     if (interrupter_()) {
         ...handle interrupt...
         ... stop ...
     }
   }

Then the question is how often we check.

One obvious choice would be to do it each time the log
probability/gradient function is called.  Or once per
sample, or once per N samples.

I don't know how slow it is, and after you call their interrupt,
we apparently can't even assume we get control back,
so we might not be able to do any cleanup like flushing
buffers and closing files (I don't know if C++ does any
of that itself -- Java does).

- Bob

I prefer explicit commands where things get
converted to a single data type for a function
rather than doing with R2WinBUGS did and allowing
a range of different input types, such as a vector
of strings that are implicitly read from the enviromment
or an explicit list.

This improves modularity immensely because the function
to converts environments plus mixed lists/vectors or whatever
is documented and tested separately and not part of the maintenance/testing
responsibility of the stan() function.  It's another function
that's independently testing. This helps immensely with
both testing and doc modularity.

I also know it's not the R way of doing things,
and I think being idiomatic in R trumps doing things
modularly.  So it's really up to the R users' judgments
here.

> I'm sort of surprised list("y"<-y, ...) doesn't work.

I agree that this aspect of the R language is confusing to newcomers to R. But the problem is that newcomers don't know much about R. And it is hard to accommodate people who don't know much about R without confusing the people who do know about R.

For all R functions the thing to the left of the equals sign is the argument name and the thing to the right is the value for that argument. For example, the first argument to the mean() function is called x

> args(mean)
function (x, ...)

This is confusing to newcomers too:

y <- rnorm(100)
mean(x = y)

while they are more comfortable with

y <- rnorm(100)
mean(y)

even though they are equivalent and the latter relies on positional matching, which is fragile when the function accepts more than one argument.

The list() function takes any number of arguments

> args(list)
function (...)

So, list(y = y, x = x) utilizes two arguments, y and x, and gives them the value of y and x in the global environment. Also valid but also confusing to newcomers would be list(a = y, b = x), which also utilizes two arguments, a and b, and gives them the value of y and x in the global environment. Newcomers are happier with list(y, x) but do not recognize that the elements of the resulting list will not have identifying names. This is verbose but fine

my_list <- list(y, x)
names(my_list) <- c("y", "x")

But the point is that RStan ultimately needs names in order to produce useful output. It isn't that hard to put a function like this into RStan

get_vars <-
  function(x) {

    if(!is.list(x)) stop("'x' must be a list")
    x <- lapply(x, get)
    return(x)
}

in which case

get_vars(list("y", "x"))

will return a list of two elements containing the values of y and x in the calling environment, but we still need names. If the list were just character strings, we could use those as names

get_vars <-
  function(x) {

    if(!is.list(x)) stop("'x' must be a list")
    if(!all(sapply(x, is.character))) stop("all elements of 'x' must be characters")
    xnames <- unlist(x)
    x <- lapply(x, get)
    names(x) <- xnames
    return(x)
}

But mixing, like

get_vars(list("N", x = y))

wouldn't work. It is probably worth putting the second version of get_vars() behind the RStan NAMESPACE so that the user can specify list("y", "x"), but better still would be for the user to learn the damn language.

Ben

>

> Yeah, that would be a pain to handle in general. Maybe the parser could spit a warning or something. But my main point
> is that interrupts are not the solution to faulty code. They are the solution to impatience with the presumed correct code.

It'd be nice if we could have both so that
a faulty model doesn't cause us to have to shut
down the R process (and lose all the work in it).

But I just don't see how to do that with any efficiency
when we compile user code.

The within-leapfrog vs. within-sample is just a granularity
issue, though one with tradeoffs among ease of coding,
efficiency, and immediate interruptibility.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 10, 2012 6:24:30 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> If we want to be able to interrupt during leapfrogging for example, then yes the check for an interrupt would need to go deeper. But I don't think interrupts are intended to make it possible to escape from an infinite loop; an infinite loop shouldn't be possible to fall into in the first place. I see interrupts as a solution for problem of "my model is taking too long and I don't care enough anymore", in which case it is probably okay to allow interrupting every sampled iteration.

To this end, it would be more useful if stan() would still return some output when interrupted, which is a bit tricky. Inside a potentially long-running function, you can do something like

interrupted <- TRUE
on.exit( if(interrupted) do_something() )
output <- run_model()
interrupted <- FALSE
return(output)

That way if the user hits the interrupt signal while run_model() is running, whatever the expression after if(interrupted) gets executed. For example, this could assign whatever posterior samples we have to the global environment with an explanatory message, e.g.

do_something <- function() {
  half_posterior <<- # whatever
  warning("You interrupted Stan before he was done. The results have been placed in the 'half_posterior' object in the global environment. Interpret with caution, if at all")
  return(invisible(NULL))
}

And if the user does not hit the interrupt signal while run_model() is running, then interrupted gets set to FALSE, in which case do_something() is not called when stan() exits.

Ben

messages.subject: slow eight schools
messages.body_plain:
I've been looking into the eight schools model, and the issue seems to
be that the longer you run a chain for the greater your chances of
getting to a place where you wind up rejecting for a long time and
screwing up your ESS. This isn't because of bad adaptation—it happens
regardless of how long you adapt for. It's a potentially interesting
phenomenon, and one worth investigating further, insofar as it seems
to contradict the conventional wisdom that the only reason to run
multiple chains is so that you can do convergence monitoring.

More on this story as it develops.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: slow eight schools
messages.body_plain:
The 8 schools (actually, any hierarchical model) actually will take forever in Metropolis or Gibbs if you get close enough to the tau=0 point.  This is discussed in my JCGS paper with David Van Dyk.

One way to solve the problem (in Gibbs/Metropolis, possibly also in HMC) is to do redundant parameterization.  I actually demonstrate that in the 8 schools case in Appendix C of BDA.  It is a mild annoyance, though.

I am expecting that one of our upcoming resarch projects (once stan is fully running) is to set up a new notation and coding for hierarchical models, in which case perhaps the redundant parameterization can be done invisibly.  Also there's the issue of saving finite-sample comparisons as quantities of intersest.  We can discuss further when we have time to think about this.

For now, I think we can accept that we have a problem that Bugs etc also have.

See you
A

messages.subject: Stan Syntax Highlighting for pygments, google-code-prettify, and listings
messages.subject_clean: Stan Syntax Highlighting for pygments, google-code-prettify, and listings
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First, I want to thank everyone for an awesome piece of software.  I benchmarked it on some dynamic linear models and it was comparable in ESS and superior in speed to
the forward filtering backward sampling implementation in the dlm package.

Since you are working on the webpage, I thought it might be nice to have syntax highlighting for Stan models.  So, I added Stan support for most of the popular pretty printing programs that produce HTML or LaTeX.
Pygments: https://github.com/jrnold/pygments_bugs
google-code-prettify: https://github.com/jrnold/prettify-lang-r-bugs
listings LaTeX package: https://github.com/jrnold/lstBUGS
I filed issues or pull-requests for both pygments (https://bitbucket.org/birkenfeld/pygments-main/pull-request/89/bugs-like-language-lexers) and prettify (http://code.google.com/p/google-code-prettify/issues/detail?id=234),
so maybe at some point they will be merged upstream and Stan models will be natively highlighted on github, googlecode, etc.

The pygments implementation is by far the most complete, and produces both LaTeX and HTML. And many static site generators, like Jekyll, have pygments support built in.   As an example, I attached the LaTeX and HTML output
for the magnesium.stan example using the default pygments style.

I really appreciate your work, and would love to be able to contribute back in any way possible.

Jeffrey Arnold
PhD candidate, Political Science, University of Rochester

messages.subject: options for slow convergence at tau=0
messages.subject_clean: options for slow convergence at tau=0
messages.body_plain:
My guess, based on my paper with Van Dyk et al., is that no step size will work if the sims happen to get close enough to 0.  The only way I can see right now to solve it are:  (a) parameter expansion, or (b) a prior that is zero at 0 and increases linearly from there in some small local region near 0.  This should have the effect of kicking the sampler away from 0, which is what we want.

On the upside, we're no worse off than Bugs etc.

Another approach would be to have a possibility that is tied to diagnostics, where if there is a place that happens to be close to the boundary (e.g., tau near 0) where nothing's accepting, that we give the user the automatic option of slapping down a prior that kicks things away from 0.  Given that these problems shoudl generally be happening at boundaries, this might actually be a reasonable option!

A

and I have fixed some bugs.

I am still working on collect more information about the sampler to R.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan float
messages.body_plain:
I agree. Not being able to interrupt a process without killing the
environment it's running in can be infuriating.

<Possibly boring examples of Matlab being infuriating>

For example, in Matlab until recently it was impossible to interrupt
audio playback, so if you accidentally forgot to specify the sampling
rate and typed
sound(signal)
instead of
sound(signal, 44100)
then you'd have to listen to your signal at the default sampling rate
of 8000 Hz, e.g., your 10-second sound file would be pitch-shifted
down by about 2.5 octaves and play for about a minute.

I still often have to quit Matlab when I accidentally type
x = zeros(100000);
(which tries to allocate a 100000-by-100000 matrix) instead of
x = zeros(100000, 1);
(which produces a 100000-by-1 vector).

</Possibly boring examples of Matlab being infuriating>

Anyway, the point is people will feel more positively about Stan if it
doesn't force them to restart R and throw away any valuable state that
they may have in their workspace.

Matt

messages.subject: Andrew's proposal for avoiding model recompilation
messages.subject_clean: Andrew's proposal for avoiding model recompilation
messages.body_plain:
Here's Andrew's proposal for avoiding model recompilation,
as far as I understood it:

1.  Each call to RStan's stan() function will be supplied with:
     -- a model name
     -- the model contents as a string or file
     -- a working directory into which results are written

2.  The model contents get written to the working directory
     in a file given by the model name.

3.  When a model's (re)compiled, we save (in some space private
     to RStan that won't get overwritten by users):
     -- the name of the model,
     -- the working directory

4.  We only compile the model if:
     -- there is no compiled model loaded at the time, or
     -- there is a compiled model loaded, but
        * the name of model is different,
        * the working directory location is different, or
        * the contents saved in the working directory don't match
          the about-to-be-compiled model contents

This should work.  (Having named directories and named models is
what I was talking about when I said we'd have to deal with
some naming conventions.)

As I understand it from Jiqiang, there's no good way to save the
shared object (.so) or dynamic linked lib (.dll) across R sessions.
So it'll have to be compiled at least once per session.

It does mean that we won't be able to bounce back and forth
among different models.  So if you run eight schools, then
speed dating in the same R session, you'll have to compile eight
schools again the next time you use it.   A more general way of
doing this might be to create a stack of model names/working dirs
in R's memory, but that would require being able to reload the
models.  Is that possible?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We've been having a discussion with a third party I
thought I'd bring onto the list.

The >> are from me and >>> and > are from Ben.

>> There's no obstacle in principle to adding sparse matrices, other than that Eigen probably doesn't support the
>> same set of operations on them, and we'd have to add a whole new set of expression templates to deal vectorizing
>> them.
>
> Right. Although with 3.1.x, they brought sparse almost up to par with dense.

That's really good news.

>>> As I've said to Bob and Andrew in the past, about the only thing  that is good about the Wishart-family priors is
>>> that they are conjugate with something, which is irrelevant unless you  are doing Gibbs sampling, which Stan is
>>> not doing. The biggest advantage of Stan's LKJ priors is that you can put a joint  uniform prior on the
>>> correlation matrix and whatever prior you want on the standard deviations, plus it is easy to  shrink the
>>> correlation prior toward the identity matrix. Other problems may have AR1 structure or something else, which Stan
>>> could easily handle but does not at the moment.
>>
>> I'm probably missing something about Stan not handling AR1 structure.
>
> Stan can do it, particularly if the user can hack the .stan file, but we don't have any awesome C++ to handle the
> covariance or correlation matrix of an AR1 process. If rho is the auto-regressive parameter, the entries of the
> correlation matrix are powers of rho. And the precision matrix is tridiagonal and known analytically. So, it would be
>  inefficient to plow that through multivariate_normal_log().

Ah -- that's what I was missing.

I'll add it to the to-do list :-)

messages.subject: Eight Schools + uniform parameter declarations/definitions
messages.body_plain:
I want to highlight something important before
getting back to Eight Schools below:

If we define sigma_theta to sample from a uniform

   sigma_theta ~ uniform(0, 1000);

then it should be declared with matching bounds, as in

   real[0,1000] sigma_theta;

It might work w/o bounds if you happen to get lucky and start
with a value in [0,1000] -- otherwise, you're in NaN land
outside of the support for sigma_theta.  You can also land
outside the support due to the random momentum of each iteration,
which is always Normal(0,1), no matter which dimension it is.

On 8/13/12 9:58 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I will change the wiki page to this version.  Essentially, in my version, I do not have prior statement for mu_theta and
> sigma_theta, as presented in chapter 5 of BDA2.

I forgot about that one.  So that's three
versions just in BDA.

I don't know where the Cauchy prior came from
because the ones in src/models were from the appendix
of BDA.  I had played around with other priors like
the Cauchy and Gamma before (following another paper of
Andrew et al.'s on hierarchical variance priors).

> Here we have those diffuse prior for mu_theta and sigma_theta just
> because BUGS and JAGS must need a prior statement for parameters.  So I think it might be a bit better that we use
>
> real sigma_theta;
>
> in the parameters block so that we could either have
>
> mu_theta ~ normal(0,1000);
> sigma_theta ~ uniform(0, 1000);
>
> or leave them out in the model block as Stan allow it.

Given that we need the declaration to be:

    real sigma_theta[0,1000];

then it's just na issue of whether we include the redundant:

    sigma_theta ~ uniform(0,1000);

It's not really even any less efficient because the implementation's
clever

messages.body_plain:
This is a bit complicated.  I propose we just maintain a table in the R's working space.  In the table, we just have columns such as

ID, stanmodel

I suppose we can create an ID from a character string of Stan model code using some hash algorithm.  After a model compiling is potentially needed, we use the ID to see if we have already compiled the model.  If yes, we just use the table to obtain the stanmodel that was compiled previously.  If no, we compile the model and put the compiled the stanmodel in the table.  I do not see a problem if we first fit a 8 schools model, then a rats model, then 8 schools again.  One issue I see now is that R allows user to delete objects and R's garbage collector could delete objects if they are used anymore, in which case I am not sure it is possible to delete records from the table.

> As I understand it from Jiqiang, there's no good way to save the
> shared object (.so) or dynamic linked lib (.dll) across R sessions.
> So it'll have to be compiled at least once per session.

Yes. All works fine just in one session.  The programmer of rstan knows the same about those shared objects as the user of rstan. We delegate the compiling of C++ code to package inline, so we do not where they are saved and when/how they loaded though we might be able to get those information if we want.  And this is the reason why we have problems with saving compiled models and reloading them.

--
Jiqiang

messages.body_plain:
If you just need the objects accessible for the session, I think you can do this with a couple lines of code using the package memoise. When you memoise a function it will cache the results for each unique input a function is called with, and when the function is called again with those same inputs it will return the cached results.  I prototyped it with cxxfunction and basic examples and it seems to work.  In the example below, it will only compile the code the first time.  The second time it immediately returns the function.

> library(memoise)
> library(RcppArmadillo)
> ## Original function
> compilefun <- function(sig, body, plugin) {
>     cxxfunction(sig, body, plugin = plugin, verbose=TRUE)
> }
> ## Memoised function
> smartcompile <- memoise(compilefun)
>
> sig1 <- signature(x="integer", y="numeric")
> body1 <- 'return ScalarReal( INTEGER(x)[0] * REAL(y)[0] ) ;'
>
> f1 <- smartcompile(sig1, body1, "default")
> f2 <- smartcompile(sig1, body1, "default")
> identical(f1, f2)
>
> sig2 <- sig1
> body2 <- 'return wrap( as<int>(x) * as<double>(y) ) ;'
> f3 <- smartcompile(sig2, body2, "Rcpp")
> f4 <- smartcompile(sig2, body2, "Rcpp")
> identical(f3, f4)

To persist objects across sessions, once the inline problem is figured out, is a lot like how the packages knitr or cacher persist the results of evaluating chunks of code, and their caching systems can probably be heavily borrowed from.

messages.body_plain:
As a suggestion which might allow things to persist across sessions why don't you use a tmp directory?  For instance, when stan() is called the directory $TMPDIR/RStan-$USERNAME/<md5sum of model contents>/ is created if it doesn't exist and is used to hold all information.  If it already exists it can be assumed that the contents corresponds to the same model.  The md5sum of the model contents ensures that if the filename or model name remains the same but the model is changed (as might happen when people are tweaking a model) it still gets recompiled.

In other words, instead of creating a table in R, you use the filesystem temp directory as a table.

Cheers,
Marcus

runs within a single session of R.  The problem again
is how objects and state get saved in R.  The dynamic
libraries aren't saved and reloaded when you reload
R.

messages.subject: schools
messages.body_plain:
Bob commented on there being multiple versions of the 8 schools so I wanted to explain what was happening.  Here's the story.
A

1.  The original 8-schools model from Rubin (1980) and chapter 5 of BDA:
y_j ~ N(theta_j, sigma^2_j) for j=1,…,J
theta_j ~ N(mu,tau^2), for j=1,…,J
p(mu,tau) proportional to 1.

2.  The Bugs parameterization used in appendix C of BDA:
For Bugs, we need to introduce a parameter for inverse-variance.  We called this tau.theta.  Then we used sigma.theta for the sd, and changed mu to mu.theta for parallelism.
We also put in proper but extremely weak priors for the hyperparameters.

I don't like model 2, and now that we've abandoned Bugs, I want to abandon model 2.
- I will go back to using tau for the group-level sd.
- I don't like those extremely weak priors.  If I'm gonna use a proper prior, I prefer something weakly informative but not super-weak.  For example, mu ~ N(0,100^2) and tau ~ half-Cauchy (0, 100).  Or maybe replacing the 100's by 25's.

3.  Redundant parameterization.  As discussed in the recent email exchange with Matt3, there are different ways of doing this.  In any case, the basic idea is to write:
theta_j = mu + xi*eta_j, for j=1,…,J
eta_j ~ N(0, tau.eta^2), for j=1,…,J
p(mu) proportional to 1
and then put priors on xi and tau.alpha.
(I'm not wedded to the notation "xi, eta, tau.eta" but we need to use something here.)

For the Stan how-to-get-started page, I would like to use model 1.

For Appendix C of the new BDA, I will want to use model 1, followed by model 3 (with details of model 3 settled after further experimentation and discussion with Matt).

On 8/14/12 6:41 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

 > This is probably impossible, butï¿½  if there are any clever

 > ways of getting compilation to be faster, that would be great!

We've already done the first-order things.

The main problem is that the compiler settings that produce
fast code are themselves slow.

Overall, with the size models you're looking at,
compiling at -O0 level and running would probably
take less time overall than compiling at -O3 level (-O is
for optimization level, with 0 minimum and 3 the max that
matters).

Here are two ways we might speedup compilation:

1.  More precompilation into object files.

Pros:  faster compiles
Cons:  it makes the code more difficult to manage
        and less flexible by requiring redundancy
        and preinstation of templates

2.  More targeted imports.

Pros:  faster compiles because less code to read
Cons:  may defeat precompiled headers

- Bob

On 8/9/12 3:25 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

>> The main reason for having these types is that we can
>> infer that for
>>
>>     row_vector * vector
>>
>> the result type is real.
>
> If you think that's a good idea, we can go with it.

Great!  I do think it's a good idea.

 > My inclination (based on my background from R) is to _not_
 > allow just plain "*" to do this.  I would prefer something more explicitly such as
> inner (a, b);
> which would return the inner product of a and b whether or not they are both row_vectors, both vectors, or one of each (in either order).  Actually, I would prefer to just have "vector" and forget about "row_vector" but I could see (perhaps) how row_vector will help when we're doing matrix multiplication.
>
> I'm not saying to go change everything right now;

I'd say it's now or never.  If we change things later,
we'll break every model that a user has written.

 > it just seems like it might be worth discussing.  My worry about "*" is the
> potential confusion, I see the code as less readable because when I see "*" I
> will have to go back to declarations to see what is what.  "inner(,)" seems more clear to me.

The way we did typing of vector, row vector and matrix
follows Eigen, which I really like.  I also like that
you get more precise type inference for expressions.

Other people prefer a more R-like way of doing things
where all the types are very squishy and interconvertible
based on what's calling them.

We could've done that in Stan. We could still do it now,
but it's going to take A LOT of work, because it touches
every aspect of Stan from the model parser to the documentation
to the models.

I haven't tried to formulate a coherent alternative
typing.  A lot of what R has to do with inner and what not
is because of the implicit type conversions they allow.

Our matrix ops are more like MATLAB.

".*" is componentwise multiplication, and * is always always
always matrix multiplication reducing to simplest type.

   (matrix * matrix):matrix
   (real * matrix):matrix
   (real * vector):vector
   (row_vector * vector):real
   (vector * row_vector):matrix

etc.

The simpler types always recombine properly under
multiplication in compound expressions.  But NOT in
assignment.

So I can't do

   matrix(1,1) x;
   row_vector(K) rv;
   vector(K) v;
   x <- rv * v;  // (rv * v) is type real

This we could add easily enough.

We could get rid of row_vector and vector and just
have matrix.  Then we'd treat row vectors and vectors
as 1 x N and M x 1 matrices.  And when you multiply
a 1 x M matrix by an M x 1 matrix, you get a 1 x 1 matrix.

>
>>
>> Do you think we'll have cause to use matrix operations on
>> integer-based matrices?
>
> Possibly.  This comes up in some models in psychometrics (and, I assume, in CS) with latent classes.  Then again, we don't know how we will be fitting such models, as HMC doesn't work there!

That we can extend to later easily, too.
We'd just have to treat real as the default.

>> There aren't any angle brackets yet -- we're just making
>> sure that the current language is extendable to something
>> reasonable.
>
> I thought you were proposing angle brackets for constrained parameters.

Just for matrices, so to declare a as an M x N matrix
of non-negative real values, it'd be:

   matrix<real[0,]>[M,N] a;

But I like

   matrix[bounds=0,][M,N] a;

better, so let's just go with that (pending the decision
to completely redesign the language!).

- Bob

messages.subject: RNG functions in models - design issues
messages.subject_clean: RNG functions in models - design issues
messages.body_plain:
We want to be able to have random number generating
functions accessible through the models.   I see
them being used in the following blocks for the following
purposes (please help me fill in things I've missed here):

   block: transformed data
   use: random data generation
   issue:  only way to save is with generated quantity
           variable set to value

   block: transformed parameters
   use:  random parameters
   issues:  transformed param block executes before model;
            inefficient to assign double values to agrad::var

   block:  model
   use:  random intermediate quantities
   issues:  no way to save (can use transformed params to save)

   block:  generated quantities
   use:  forward sampling
   issues:  none

There are three relevant blocks in the generated code for the model:

    constructor() reading data and transforming data
    log_prob()    computation
    write_csv()   transforming params and generating the generated quantities

The model doesn't hold a reference to the random number generator
used by the sampler -- the sampler does.  In this case, the hmc_base
base class holds the random number generators.  The samplers then call
the constructor once to create the model, including reading data and
generating transformed data.  The log_prob() function is called repeatedly
during the leapfrog iterations.  The write_csv() function is called
once per iteration to do the write.

This just seems odd to me -- having both non-deterministic data
and a non-deterministic log prob.  The non-deterministic log prob
means successive calls to log_prob with RNGs in different states
can produce different answers.  That's only possible if we allow
randomization in transformed parameters.

So the sampler would have to pass in an RNG to these functions
as an argument.  We can't put the RNG in the model itself, because
the model's set up to be called concurrently from multiple threads,
but RNGs aren't thread safe.  (The L'Ecuyer setup uses different
samplers in different threads that are initialized to be independent.)

A remaining issue is whether to specify the RNG argument as a reference
or as a pointer.  Pointers give us the option of passing 0 in the
case the log prob function doesn't need an RNG.  On the other hand,
simple Boost RNGs are very cheap to construct from a simple seed
and you only need to do it once, so I'm inclined to go with a reference.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'd add a new block as a future use case for the random number generation capability.

block: parameter initialization
use: random initialization of parameters, potentially based on data
issues: none that I can see

This is highly relevant for time-series models where, given the parameters of a time series, it makes no sense to sample the state variables of the time series independently.

Anything which makes log_prob() non-deterministic seems like trouble to me and probably should be avoided.  What's the real use case for sampling in the transformed parameters?  I can't think of a valid use for this.  I can see the use for randomly perturbed (or generated) data, but I'm not certain it's necessary as most people using Stan will be getting their data from other environments (eg, R, Matlab, etc) which can happily synthesize data.

Cheers,
Marcus

This sounds fine to me but I am still processing some of these ideas.  Let me just ask some questions:

1.  I'm trying to understand "<-" expressions, that is, expressions of the form a <- …
Is it corret that, in such expressions, the thing on the left of the "<-" can be an intermediate quantity (a "local variable" in the model) or a transformed perameter, but that's it?  Thta is, you can't have data or parameters to the left of "<-"?

2.  Would it be legal for a model to have multiple distribution calls for a parameter or for data?  For example:
y ~ normal (0, 1)
y ~ normal (0, 2)
My guess, from my understanding of the model, is that the above two lines would be ok; they would just add two factors to the posterior density.  Thats actually fine with me, I have no desire for Stan to forbid such specifications.  I just want to check that I'm understandging things correctly.

3.  I still find the "transformed paraameter" thing to be awkward but maybe that's the only way to do it.  What is confusing me is that I see there being two reasons for defining transformed parameters:  (a) simple post-processing.  For example, we define theta[1] <- exp(phi[1])/(exp(phi[1])+exp(phi[2])+exp(phi[3])), etc.; (b) we want to save some intermediate quantities in the computation.

I bring up transformed parameters because I see something similar happening with generated quantities, for example in (manual) posterior predictive checks where we simulate y_rep.  Given how Stan works, it's definitely important to define y_rep as a generated quantity rather than simply as another parameter in the model.  But, as with transformed parameters, this is a computational thing.  To a statistician, y_rep is just one more unknown quantity.
