messages.body_plain:
Changing the approach to matrix typing at this point
would be a HUGE hassle.  I also have a strong preference
for the way it is.  One thing we could do is add
other functions.  For instance, there's already a dot
function that will do dot products of any pair of vectors
(not arrays).  This again follows Eigen's lead.

I'm ambivalent about naming bounds or rows/columns.
Since Andrew feels strongly about naming just
bounds, why don't we do that?  The change to the parser
is trivial and I can pretty automatically change the
models.  Just to remind everyone, that's:

    real[bounds=0,1] x;

instead of

    real[0,1] x;

Basically, the syntax just inserts a "bounds" and then "="
token before the bounds.  So that's trivial.

It also clears the way for doing matrices in a reasonable
way, with

    matrix[bounds=-1,1][3,4] x;

I slightly prefer Marcus's suggested syntax:

    matrix<real[0,1]>[3,4] x;

I don't have any trouble keeping track of the fact
that angle brackets are for type information and square
brackets for size info.   But we do have to do something
so we don't wind up with the too-confusing notation:

    matrix[0,1][3,4] x;

To allow matrices of int values, we'd probably use something
like:

    matrix[scalar=int, bounds=1,5][3,4] n;

I don't like the overload of the comma here, but I can already
hear Andrew's voice saying he'll never be able to keep
the use of semicolons straight if we did something like:

    matrix[scalar=int; bounds=1,5][3,4] n;

and that it's too much notation with more cleanly
delineated subexpressions as in:

    matrix[scalar=int; bounds=[1,5]][3,4] n;

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 8/15/12 4:52 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> This sounds fine to me but I am still processing some of these ideas.  Let me just ask some questions:
>

> 1.  I'm trying to understand "<-" expressions, that is, expressions of the form a <- ï¿½

> Is it corret that, in such expressions, the thing on the left of the "<-" can be an intermediate quantity (a "local variable" in the model) or a transformed perameter, but that's it?  Thta is, you can't have data or parameters to the left of "<-"?

The manual lays all of this out in gory detail.

On the left of an "<-" you can have any variable declared
in the block in which the "<-" shows up, including local
variables.

So you get transformed data vars on the left of <- in
the transformed data block, transformed parameter vars
on the left of <- in the transformed parameter block,
generated quantities on the left of <- in the generated
quantities block, and you can always have a local
variable (standard name, no scare quotes) on the left side
of <- in any statement block.

> 2.  Would it be legal for a model to have multiple distribution calls for a parameter or for data?  For example:
> y ~ normal (0, 1)
> y ~ normal (0, 2)
> My guess, from my understanding of the model, is that the above two lines would be ok; they would just add two factors to the posterior density.  Thats actually fine with me, I have no desire for Stan to forbid such specifications.  I just want to check that I'm understandging things correctly.

Yes, that's what happens.  There's a to-do item to issue
a warning if a user does this, but I haven't coded it yet.
the problem is figuring out when it's really the same variable
if you have an expression for an index, as with

    for (n in 1:2) y[n] ~ normal(0,1);
    for (n in 3:4) y[n] ~ normal(0,1);

Here there's no conflict, but if you replace n with a more
complex expression, it gets hard to tell at compile time whether
you'll assign once or twice.

> 3.  I still find the "transformed paraameter" thing to be awkward but maybe that's the only way to do it.  What is confusing me is that I see there being two reasons for defining transformed parameters:  (a) simple post-processing.  For example, we define theta[1] <- exp(phi[1])/(exp(phi[1])+exp(phi[2])+exp(phi[3])), etc.; (b) we want to save some intermediate quantities in the computation.

> I bring up transformed parameters because I see something similar happening with generated quantities, for example in (manual) posterior predictive checks where we simulate y_rep.  Given how Stan works, it's definitely important to define y_rep as a generated quantity rather than simply as another parameter in the model.  But, as with transformed parameters, this is a computational thing.  To a statistician, y_rep is just one more unknown quantity.

I'm open to alternatives, but this is the best I could
come up with.

They were designed for the following usage pattern, which
I tried to make clear in the manual:

   +use in model, +print:  transformed parameter
   +use in model, -print:  local variable
   -use in model, +print:  generated quantity

For a statistician, the key is +/- use in model.
Generated quantities, while they're just "one more
unknown quantity", by definition don't affect the joint
log probability over the parameters.

- Bob

statements both in the model and in the generated quantities,

>   }

>     ...
>     y_rep ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>     ...
>
>   }
>

Ah, I see.  I think that repetition of code will be really hard to avoid though unless something like macros are added to the syntax.  If we wanted to do fairly powerful macros in a cheap and cheerful way we could use the C preprocessor :)

We could write our own little preprocessor
for #include.  We could also use C's as Marcus
suggests, which would give us that for free.
The biggest issue is dealing with things like line
numbers in error output.  The parser's taking
in a string iterator with line number tracking, and
it's not sophisticated enough to know it's in a
subfile.  We'd have to do something like translate
the error outputs.

I'm very anti-macro, though, as it makes things
very hard to debug, even if we get line numbers right.

I'd rather introduce simple macro-like function
definitions.  If we have syntax that's context dependent,
the issue is whether we could reuse it or not.

- Bob

> > The C preprocessor is completely distinct from the rest of the compiler and can be used separately to use #include,
> > #define, #if, etc.  In fact, you can do this already with a script.  For instance:
> >
> > cpp -I<incdir> model-withmacros.stan model.stan
> > stanc model.stan
> > ...
> >
> > The call to cpp could be done directly in stanc if we wanted to support that functionality directly but you can also

>
> I knew it was possible, but didn't realize it
> was this easy -- the C++ compilers let
> you see all sorts of intermediate stages of the
> work they do.
>
> I'm very tempted NOT to mention this in manuals,
> etc., and leave it to the C whizzes to do on their
> own.  The only issue is that then their models
> wouldn't work in the in the R interface.  (Maybe
> we could put an expert mode expand macros in or
> something.)

The brute force approach is to call cpp with a system call from the parser to produce a temp file which gets parsed per usual.  More sophisticated (although perhaps more work?) is to use something like Wave (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_50_0/libs/wave/index.html).  I'm not sure how it fits into the existing parser framework, but given that it's part of boost, it may work well.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, August 16, 2012 6:31:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm going to lead with the issue that's bugging me and then
> get to Ben's post on Windows 8.
>
> How much of the following space do we want to test and support:
>
>     OS version  x  bit size  x  compiler  x  library version

At some point, we just have to let users be our testers, and if Stan doesn't work for some combination of the above that users might have, they know where to find us. That said, there is a lot of value for us to be able to say on the website that the following combinations passed our unit tests (and possibly model tests) on $DATE. That would encourage users with the same or similar combinations to download Stan and find out whether that still holds.

(Tangent: Perhaps the binary version(s) of Stan could come with a testme executable?)

And all that said, we have been really, really lucky or good in the sense that we haven't had a major compilation problem on any attempted OS, bitness, compiler version, and library version since Jenkins got Rtools, and I believe we did it without a single ifdef hack in the Stan code.

> Here's what I know about:

In addition, you have Sun / Oracle hardware (where Stan will probably work with a recent g++ but definitely not with the Sun / Oracle compiler), various *BSD systems (where Stan will probably work if it works on a Mac), and in the near-future, if not already, ARM-based tablets (where Stan could work but likely does not at the moment).

> Is it possible to set up virtual machines to do all this?

Yes, although the Apple Cops might seize any non-Apple hardware that was running a virtualized Apple OS.

> How do we create a VM and which hardware/OS do we need?

I think any hardware / OS combination is fine, except the aforementioned non-Apple / Apple one and 32bit native hardware / 64bit OS. A VM program like

https://www.virtualbox.org/

allows you to create a VM from either a physical CD / DVD that installs the OS or an .iso file of said CD / DVD.

Ben

On 8/17/12 1:50 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I was amused to come across this:
> http://andrewgelman.com/2008/05/axes_that_exten/
> which anticipates some of what we're doing with upper and lower bounds in Stan.

That's eerily prescient, right down to the defaults for matrices:

   What I think would be better is for every data object to have
   a ï¿½typeï¿½ attached: the type could be integer, nonnegative integer,
   positive integer, continuous, nonnegative continuous, binary, discrete
   with bounded range, discrete with specified labels, unordered discrete,
   continuous between 0 and 1, etc. If the type is not specified (i.e., NULL),
   it could default to unconstrained continuous

One thing we don't have is named categorical
outcomes.  Everything is just integers.

I'm a big believer in strong type systems.  Both of my
books have "type" in the title.

I'm just tidying up the named bounds and then I'll push
through changes to the models, web docs, and manual.

I didn't add upper/lower bounds for matrices or integer
matrices yet, but both are doable with some work.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: won't work: Boost Wave as standalone macro preprocessor
messages.body_plain:
Looks like we can't use Boost Wave as a standalone
preprocessor because it's tied into the C lexer.

Here's a query to the Boost Spirit mailing list and a reply from
Hartmut Kaiser, the developer:

   > Yes the use case is Use wave as **only** for preprocessing ...
   > I need to iterate characters and some direction on writing the NEW
   > iterator.

   Sorry that does not work. You can't use Wave for preprocessing only. It is
   built on top of a tokenizer (lexer) and operates itself with tokens.

- Bob

messages.subject: 25% of time spent in check_range?
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

So I'm playing with a simple model in Stan and it was running a bit slower than I would have expected.  After a profiling run, it turned out that around 25% of the time was being spent in check_range().  I would have expected that these checks would have been disabled with -DNDEBUG at compile time (which turns off these checks in Eigen), but apparently not.  An easy fix is to wrap the body of check_range with an #ifndef NDEBUG block.

Anyone have any thoughts?  For reference, this was with clang++ and -O3 on Linux.

messages.body_plain:
On 8/17/12 4:39 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Hey,
>
> So I'm playing with a simple model in Stan and it was running a bit slower than I would have expected.  After a
> profiling run, it turned out that around 25% of the time was being spent in check_range().  I would have expected that
> these checks would have been disabled with -DNDEBUG at compile time (which turns off these checks in Eigen), but
> apparently not.  An easy fix is to wrap the body of check_range with an #ifndef NDEBUG block.
>
> Anyone have any thoughts?  For reference, this was with clang++ and -O3 on Linux.

My first thought is "yikes".

My second thought is that we've found g++ to
be a bit faster.

My third thought is that putting in flags is a good
idea that we should finally get around to doing!

I think we should follow Eigen, which turns off range
checking if either the flag NDEBUG or flag EIGEN_NO_DEBUG
is used (i.e., called with -DNDEBUG or -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG).

So I'd suggest STAN_NO_DEBUG and calling the error checking
under the condition that !(STAN_NO_DEBUG || NDEBUG).

We'd then want to be able to pass options through calls
to stanc.  That in turn means we can't precompile object
files for the relevant calls, at least if we turn things
off at a fairly low level.

I'm curious as to why it's so expensive.  The function
is inline, passes three size_t values and a const char*,
with a body that's a simple if statement that's
always false.  I wonder if it's somehow
opportunistically pre-allocating for the stringstream?
Or the size is causing it not to be inlined.
Just in case, I broke out a raise_range_error.

So it now looks like this:

     void raise_range_error(size_t max,
                              size_t i,
                              const char* msg,
                              size_t idx) {
           std::stringstream s;
           s << "INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS"
             << "; index=" << i
             << "; lower bound=1"
             << "; upper bound=" << max
             << "; index position=" << idx
             << "; " << msg
             << std::endl;
           throw std::out_of_range(s.str());
       }

       inline
       void check_range(size_t max,
                        size_t i,
                        const char* msg,
                        size_t idx) {
         if (i < 1 || i > max)
           raise_range_error(max,i,msg,idx);
       }

I pushed the change.

Should the test for NDEBUG or STAN_NO_DEBUG be on the
body of check range as Marcus suggests?  That would be my
inclination because it should be sufficient
to make sure check_range is inlined away.  We just have
to be sure not to precompile check_range if we do it
this way!

We can also turn off checks in the probability
functions the same way.  Some of those will be expensive
if we test that matrices are positive definite, etc.

- Bob

Wait until you have g++ configured to use -O3 (see
Jiqiang's latest directions for RStan on how to do
this).

The run times are much faster, but compile time slows
to a crawl.

So it's a tradeoff depending on what you want to do.

If you have a big model and know it works, -O3 on g++ is
the way to go.  Otherwise, I've just been using -O0.

For something like 8 Schools, which is trivial, you won't
notice the slowdown in runtime, but you will notice the
speedup in compile time going from -O2 to -O0.

At least one plus is that most of our syntax errors
are found in the stanc model translation phase.  Everything
stanc translates should at least compile in C++.

messages.subject: restricted order of lower=, upper=
messages.body_plain:
In order to get Stan to compile on Windows,
I reduced the grammar complexity so that only
the following are legal:

    int<lower=L,upper=U>
    int<lower=L>
    int<upper=U>

Two cases from the fully general definition are
missing:

    int<upper=U,lower=L>
    int<>

Ditto for "real".

Although it doesn't seem like much, it cut down
on the complexity of the grammar rules.

The question is whether we want to allow the
backwards order.  I see some benefit in eliminating
the two cases that are missing.

Also, should I do the same thing for truncation,
as in converting

    y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,];

to

    y ~ normal(0,1) T<lower=1>;

I prefer the interval notation, because the angle
brackets evoke type constraints for me due to
C++ and Java.

- Bob

This might be ok sometimes, but it probably won't be in general.
Consider the scenario where the initial momentum for y is large
compared to the momenta for the other variables. y is going to get a
good running start in some random direction, and the other variables'
trajectories are going to take a little while to turn around. But by
the time they do, the overall trajectory will be dominated by the y
dimension, so we'll never satisfy the u-turn criterion, so each
iteration runs until we reach max_treedepth.

Basically, improper posteriors are always trouble.

Matt

messages.subject: under-/overflow, constant bounds, and gradients
messages.body_plain:
There's a question below the setoff.

As I looked at the lower/upper-bound constraint code,
I also noticed that there are two different definitions
of the ouptut.

Each transform function has two variants, one with
a log prob argument for Jacobians and one without.
The one with Jacobians is used during the log prob
calc at each leapfrog step. The one without Jacobians
is used to produce output once per iteration.

For lower/upper bound, the one without the log prob
can underflow to 0 or overflow to 1.  At some point,
Matt (I think) changed the one with the log prob argument
so that it never goes to 0 or to 1.

I brought the one without log prob into line so it
produces the same answer.

An issue with the the one with log prob that bounds
properly between 0 and 1 is that if it hits the bound
and returns a constant, the tie to the gradient is
broken.  If we'd calculated the gradient, it would have
underflowed to 0, too.

QUESTION:  Should we also build in a small gradient?

It'd make sense to build in the auto-dif for these functions.
As is, we're just relying on the expressions, and they're
pretty complex, especailly if the bounds are variables.

- Bob

messages.subject: geometry? negative binomial model unstable
messages.body_plain:
The negative binomial malloc/free error case is more puzzling.
We hadn't ever used the negative binomial before (at least not
in BUGS examples), so it hasn't been field tested.

The following model winds up with alpha, beta going to +infinity
then segfaulting on a bad free (the seg fault needs to be fixed
as well as the model's bad behavior).

  data {
     int<lower=1> N;
     int<lower=0> y[N];
   }
   parameters {
     real<lower=0.0> alpha;
     real<lower=0.0> beta;
   }
   model {
     for (i in 1:N)
       y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta);
   }

And here's the data:

   y <- c(0, 1, 4, 0, 2, 2, 5, 0, 1)
   N <- 9

The sample mean is 5/3.

This is similar to what I get from Stan if I
hard code the scale term alpha = 1 (that is, beta
around 3/5).

Even so, it's still unstable and has memory errors
with different seeds.

If I constrain alpha and beta to be above 0.1, it doesn't
crash, but adaptation takes forever and the values
of alpha and beta still tend to +infinity.

If I constrain alpha, beta to the interval (0.1,10),
everything runs fine and the estimates for alpha range
from around 1 to around 9.5 with betas around the
sample mean.

If I only constrain on (0,10), I get problems
with memory again (perhaps NaN issues on
some kind of underflow?)

Everything's also stable if I reparameterize to
probability of success and use a strong enough
location=0.5 beta prior.

Is this another geometry issue?

- Bob

messages.subject: fixed lgamma-based crashes (from neg_binomial)
messages.body_plain:
The problem was that an exception was being thrown
during the lgamma_vari constructor by Boost's lgamma
implementation.  Daniel and I pulled the lgamma
calc out of the constructor, and now everything works
fine.

That negative binomial model doesn't crash any
more, but the model itself still doesn't work.

But I think that's just HMC, not a bug.  We should
probably build some example negative binomial models
that work.

- Bob

messages.subject: negative binomial mystery solved
messages.body_plain:
Figured it out. It's a numerical problem. The negative binomial log-pdf is

lgamma(alpha+x) - lgamma(alpha)
+ alpha * log(beta) - (alpha + x) * log(beta + 1)
- lgamma(x+1).

When alpha and beta are O(1e16), effectively alpha+x=alpha and
beta+1=beta. Then the first two lines disappear, and the result
becomes independent of alpha and beta. I'm rewriting
neg_binomial_log() and binomial_coefficient_log() to be more
numerically stable using Stirling's approximation

lgamma(x+1) = x*log(x) - x + 0.5*log(2*pi*x) + 1/(12*x) ...

and the identity

a*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha)
= a*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha/(alpha+x))
= (a - b) * log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha/(alpha+x))

I'll let you know when it's pushed.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] negative binomial mystery solved
messages.body_plain:
It turns out I spoke too soon. There's a statistical issue in addition
to the numerical issue.

We're using the gamma-mixture parameterization, which says that
y ~ neg_binomial(α, β)
is equivalent to
z ~ gamma(α, β)
y ~ Poisson(z).
Suppose α=1e1000 and β=2e1000. Then this model basically reduces to
y ~ Poisson(1/2),
since the std deviation of z is 0.5e-500. (I think that's
right--anyway, it's basically 0.)

The problem is that when you put a uniform prior on alpha and beta you
wind up with an improper posterior, since you can make alpha and beta
as large as you want and still have the data be within the realm of
plausibility as long as the ratio alpha/beta doesn't get crazy.

So this isn't a valid model--you absolutely, positively need a prior.
On the plus side, I know a lot more about the negative binomial than I
used to!

I'll push the changes regardless, along with a cutoff that turns the
negative-binomial into the equivalent Poisson when alpha/beta^2 gets
small enough.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] negative binomial mystery solved
messages.body_plain:
> Given our previous problem with gamma mixtures in the Cauchy,
> I was wondering if that would be a problem.

I think this is a pretty different kind of problem than slow sampling
for the Cauchy. There, we're just up against the standard
computational challenges of MCMC with heavy-tailed distributions.
Here, we're up against the (impossible) challenge of sampling from an
improper distribution.

This issue brings up sort of an interesting question for these sorts
of heavy-tailed distributions in general. For example, what's an
appropriate non-informative prior on the number of degrees of freedom
of a t? Clearly not uniform(0,∞), since that's going to run into
exactly the same problem. The crux of the issue is that, for any
positive c, under that improper prior
p(degrees of freedom > c) = 1
p(data | degrees of freedom > c) > 0
so
p(degrees of freedom > c | data) = 1.

So what's a non-informative prior for that degrees-of-freedom
parameter? What's a weakly informative prior?

Matt

>
> So what's a non-informative prior for that degrees-of-freedom

If you had a belief about the mean degrees of freedom, then the maximum entropy distribution in this case is exponential.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_entropy_probability_distribution#Positive_and_given_mean:_the_exponential_distribution

Without a belief about the mean, I don't think there is a maximum entropy distribution in this case.

messages.body_plain:
Ok, I've pushed it along with the small change to the documentation.

If the user provides a model name with the --name parameter, then that
is used, otherwise it will strip the directories and file extension
from the model filename and append _model to the result.  That string
will then have any invalid characters replaced with _.  Hence

stanc test-file.stan

will have a model name of test_file_model.

I also added a check for user specified model names to ensure they
don't have illegal characters.  It's not, however, checking for
reserved words.  E.G.,

stanc --name=model-name

will produce an error while

stanc --name=class

will not (although the resulting code wouldn't compile.

Marcus

messages.subject: fixed issue with mean, variance, and sd
messages.subject_clean: fixed issue with mean, variance, and sd
messages.body_plain:
I just pushed a patch that fixes the mean, variance
and sd issue brought to our attention by dynotec
on the user's mailing list.  Thanks again for the report.

The fix is available as of now in the Git repository,
but it'll take some time to push through to RStan
and the source tarball.

We're really hoping to release the official 1.0
version next week (while it's still August!).
After that, we'll be tracking which bug fixes go in
which releases more closely.

(For the stan-dev x-post: The root cause was using a double
rather than the template parameter for accumulators and using
a double rather than promoting the template param for return
type. I also added unit tests and error handling for size
boundary issues, such as trying to take the sample mean
of a length zero vector or the sample variance of
a length one vector.)

- Bob

messages.subject: minor thing
messages.body_plain:
J

In the print() output from rstan, instead of Mean, SE.Mean, SD, … , ESS, Rhat,
let's change to mean, se_mean, sd, …, n_eff, Rhat.
I prefer lower case (except for Rhat, which is special), and also we should be consistent with Stan and use underscore rather than dot as a separator.  Finally, I prefer n_eff to ESS, because ESS in R can remind people of Emacs Speaks Statistics which is a distraction.

Also, can we add another line where we automatically save and summarize the log posterior (as computed by the model, up to an arbitrary normalizing constant)?  R2WinBUGS computed deviance but that's more complicated as it needs to know which parts of the model are the prior and which are the likelihood.  For now let's just keep things simple and save log posterior.

Thx
A

messages.body_plain:
On 8/23/12 7:22 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > Sometime recently, I've become unable to link the "Getting Started" example:

The two variables that your linker is choking on are
global variables defined in agrad.hpp.

   anon_model.cpp:(.text+0x4798): undefined reference to `stan::agrad::var_stack_'
   anon_model.cpp:(.text+0x47b5): undefined reference to `stan::agrad::memalloc_'

It's the only place we use global variables.

The declarations in agrad.hpp are now marked as "extern",
with the unmarked declarations in agrad.cpp.  In fact,
that's all that's in agrad.cpp other than an include of
agrad.hpp.

I'm not sure why you're having an issue linking it.
It's fine on the Mac and Windows.

If I try to declare (rather than extern) the variables in
agrad.hpp and leave agrad.cpp as a shell that only has
the include, the linker bombs with multiple definitions
across translation units.  Which is confusing to me because
there are other class definitions in agrad.hpp (though not
any bare function definitions).

- Bob

P.S.  With the latest patch to stanc, the model name will
       be based on the class name.  I'm about to modify the doc.

messages.body_plain:
It might be useful to include a template Makefile for building models in the documentation. Then the instructions are simply (1) copy the makefile  the directory with the Stan model, (2) edit some variables at the top of the makefile, and (3) run make. I know the first time I tried compiling a model, I ended up having to look through the makefile to get it to work.  Below, I pasted what I am currently using as a Makefile.

Regarding the Boost/Eigen versions in the LaTeX, you can define a macro with the current version that is being used \newcommand{\BoostVer}{1.51} and then use that macro for all the mentions in the documentation.

> # Directory of models
> SRC_DIR = .
> # Output directory
> OUT_DIR = ./
> # Location of stan
> STAN_HOME = $(HOME)/remotes/stan
> # Extension name for compiled objects
> EXE = .stanx
>
> # Compiler to use
> CC = g++
> # Level of optimization
> O = 3
>
> # DO NOT EDIT below that line
> ###################################################################################
>
> # Create objects
> source = $(wildcard $(SRC_DIR)/*.stan)
> # TODO: slash direction would need to be generalized for cross-platform.
> objects = $(addprefix $(OUT_DIR)/,$(notdir $(patsubst %.stan,%$(EXE),$(source))))
>
> # TODO: insert OS specific stuff
> AR = ar
>
> # Stan Paths
> STAN_BIN = $(STAN_HOME)/bin/
> STAN_SRC = $(STAN_HOME)/src/
> STAN_LIB = $(STAN_HOME)/lib/
> STANC = $(STAN_BIN)/stanc
>
> # Library locations
> # Kind of robust to version changes
> # and multiple versions (taking one, and usually the last one)
> EIGEN ?= $(lastword $(sort $(wildcard $(STAN_LIB)/eigen_*)))
> BOOST ?= $(lastword $(sort $(wildcard $(STAN_LIB)/boost_*)))
>
> ##
> # Set default compiler options.
> ##
> CFLAGS = -I $(STAN_SRC) -I $(EIGEN) -I $(EIGEN)/unsupported -I $(BOOST) -O$O -fPIC
> LDLIBS = -L$(STAN_BIN) -lstan
> LDLIBS_STANC = -L$(STAN_BIN) -lstanc
>
> %.cpp : %.stan
> @echo ''
> @echo '--- Translating Stan graphical model to C++ code ---'
> $(STANC) --name=$(basename $(notdir $<)) --o=$@ $<
>
> %.o : %.cpp
> @echo ''
> @echo '--- Compiling C++ code ---'
> $(COMPILE.c) $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $<
>
> %$(EXE) : %.o
> @echo ''
> @echo '--- Linking C++ model ---'
> $(LINK.c) $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $< $(LDLIBS)
>
> all: $(objects)
>
> .SECONDARY:
>
> clean:
> -rm -f $(MODEL_DIR)/*.cpp $(MODEL_DIR)/*.$(EXE) $(MODEL_DIR)/*.o

messages.subject: contributed/unsupported models & code
messages.body_plain:
We need to decide what steps to take for (a) copyright
and (b) distribution/organization for contributed code.

I'm not a lawyer, but I'm under the impression that
the original contributing author owns what
they do  unless they explicitly sign it over to the
project.

1.  What to do about small patches that people send us?
------------------------------------------------------
These are tiny fixes to the existing code base, like
an extra make target or a print routine or something
simple.  Usually a few lines of code in the form of a
Git patch.

We have to make these part of the main Stan branch
and thus governed under Stan's BSD license.
Should we get a copyright waiver and keep them on
file somewhere?

These come with data which may have its own IP issues.

We could perhaps leave the copyright with the original
owners.  I'd want to insist on open-source licensing,
though.

-----------------------------------------------------
Here, I'm thinking about things like the syntax highlighters
that we don't want to commit to maintaining ourselves
going forward, but would like to make available to our
users because we think they're cool or useful.

We could also leave these copyright with the original owners.

For (2) and (3), we can set up something like Eigen's
unsupported/ subdirectory.

messages.body_plain:
Now that Daniel got the code, I realized that Michael M
set up a Ruby-based content management and web page
server system.

I have a VERY STRONG preference for making the web
site plain old static HTML.

I'm happy to do the CSS styling to make it look
like what you (Michael M) created.

My thinking is that

1.  I don't want to have to worry about learning,
maintaining, porting, etc., a Ruby application, and

2.  I like to be able to view the web pages on my local
machine the way they will look on the web.  This carries
over to people who download Stan.

I also want to be able to keep the content under
version control, but we could probably do that with
the Ruby app.

It also looks like the default setting for the thing you
sent is blog-like.  We want to just dish up static content.
We always want "what is Stan" at the top, followed by
"download latest", etc.

If we add a news page, that should be managed like a blog.

- Bob

It's definitely a tradeoff.  I just prefer the opposite.
It reminds me of discussions of Word vs. LaTeX
or Linux vs. Windows.  I don't think there's one-size-fits-all
answer.  Nor is there for our simple web site needs.

Serving more complex and more dynamic content
definitely requires both a content management system
and a content server.  Typically it also requires
writing custom HTML, CSS and Javascript for richer
AJAX clients.

> reason to expect to be served not opened.

Ben sent a comment agreeing with you on that
front.

 > But, do what you want.

server software for HTML.

I'm a terrible sys-admin and it drives me insane doing
it.

The web provider, pair.com <http://pair.com>, lets us run code on our virtual
server.

Does someone want to volunteer to:

1.  set up whatever server code's necessary on pair.com <http://pair.com> and

2.  maintain it going forward?

I'm also happy to help

3.  modify the content so that it matches what's currently
     on mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>.

If someone else wants to do this, especially (2), I'm
happy to give it a try.

For 3, I'm particularly worried about being able to have
a simplified home page w/o nav bars, etc.

messages.subject: priors for df for t
messages.body_plain:
Also there's the question of parameterization.  It does not necessarily make sense to have independent priors on the df and scale parameters.  In some sense, the meaning of the scale parameter changes with the df.

On Aug 22, 2012, at 4:35 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:

>
> This issue brings up sort of an interesting question for these sorts
> of heavy-tailed distributions in general. For example, what's an
> appropriate non-informative prior on the number of degrees of freedom
> of a t? Clearly not uniform(0,∞), since that's going to run into
> exactly the same problem. The crux of the issue is that, for any
> positive c, under that improper prior
> p(degrees of freedom > c) = 1
> p(data | degrees of freedom > c) > 0
> so
> p(degrees of freedom > c | data) = 1.
>
> So what's a non-informative prior for that degrees-of-freedom
> parameter? What's a weakly informative prior?
>
> Matt
>

> --
>

For function *arguments*, periods are not the worst thing in the world. For function *names*, periods are pretty bad because periods are also used to indicate methods of S3 generic functions, e.g. mean.matrix() is the function that gets called by mean() when passed a matrix. It is unfortunate that R did this for 10 years so that people got used to it, and unfortunate that ESS was written when underscores were illegal in the R language so that pressing underscore results in the <- sign. But I personally don't put periods in function names ever.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure we want to die if we ever see a +-inf. There are two cases:
1. p(|θ_i|=∞) > 0
2. p(|θ_i|=∞) = 0.
Case 1 says we've got an improper posterior, and we should die in that
case. But case 2 just says that we've done a bad job of choosing a
step size, and so our leapfrog integrator has gone bananas. That's not
necessarily a huge deal, especially in the adaptation phase, so we
shouldn't do anything drastic. We could report it, though, if it's not
much of a pain.

Agree/disagree?

Matt

messages.body_plain:
We're talking about arguments to the stan() function,
not model parameters.

So things like n.burnin and n.thin in R2WinBugs.

I'd just as soon not use dots myself.  I find
them very confusing.  Ben made a very good case
for not using them for function names at least.

It would probably be simplest to just match the
command-line argument names.  Here they are,
as printed by the --help option:

   --help              Display this information

   --data=<file>       Read data from specified dump-format file
                           (required if model declares data)

   --init=<file>       Use initial values from specified file or zero values if <file>=0
                           (default is random initialization)

   --samples=<file>    File into which samples are written
                           (default = samples.csv)

   --append_samples    Append samples to existing file if it exists
                           (does not write header in append mode)

   --seed=<int>        Random number generation seed
                           (default = randomly generated from time)

   --chain_id=<int>    Markov chain identifier
                           (default = 1)

   --iter=<+int>       Total number of iterations, including warmup
                           (default = 2000)

   --warmup=<+int>     Discard the specified number of initial samples
                           (default = iter / 2)

   --thin=<+int>       Period between saved samples after warm up
                           (default = max(1, floor(iter - warmup) / 1000))

   --refresh=<+int>    Period between samples updating progress report print
                           (default = max(1,iter/200)))

   --leapfrog_steps=<int>
                       Number of leapfrog steps; -1 for No-U-Turn adaptation
                           (default = -1)

   --max_treedepth=<int>
                       Limit NUTS leapfrog steps to 2^max_tree_depth; -1 for no limit
                           (default = 10)

   --epsilon=<float>   Initial value for step size, or -1 to set automatically
                           (default = -1)

   --epsilon_pm=<[0,1]>
                       Sample epsilon +/- epsilon * epsilon_pm
                           (default = 0.0)

   --equal_step_sizes  Use same step size for every parameter with NUTS
                           (default is to estimate varying step sizes during warmup)

   --delta=<+float>    Initial step size for step-size adaptation
                           (default = 0.5)

   --gamma=<+float>    Gamma parameter for dual averaging step-size adaptation
                           (default = 0.05)

   --save_warmup       Save the warmup samples

   --test_grad         Test gradient calculations using finite differences

- Bob

messages.subject: bug in io/writer.hpp:ordered_unconstrain
messages.body_plain:
I was going through adding code for a positive_ordered type and I
think I've found a bug in io/writer.hpp:ordered_unconstrain.
Specifically, that function returns x[0] = log(y[0]) but the entries
of the ordered vector y don't need to be positive, hence y[0] could be
negative.  I'm pretty certain this is a bug but it's possible I've
missed something.

Also, I'm almost finished implementing the positive_ordered type.
Ideally we would implement ordered<lower=??,upper=??> but that's more
complexity than I know how to deal with in the parser so in the
meantime I'm just implementing the positive case.

Cheers,
Marcus

Here's my concern:  the user (such as me) who goes to Getting Started and follows the instructions and then wonders:  "Hey, do I also need to download the Latest Downloads too?"

Malecki's page looks fine to me.  But I'd like to make it clear that the way for a new user (or even a new developer, at first) to proceed is to follow the Getting Started instructions, without having to worry about the Download.

So, in the Malecki page, I think it's necessary to slightly redesign so that Getting Started is special rather than merely items 2,3,4 on a small-print list.  Perhaps, for example, Getting Started could be the permanently top item on the bloglike space on the left side of the webpage, and this item would include links to Getting Started with Stan from R, Getting Started with Stan from the Command Line, and Getting Started with Stan Using C++ (I don't actually understand the difference between these last two, but maybe I don't need to).

messages.subject: synch RStan/Stan + major.minor.patch numbering
messages.body_plain:
I'm very psyched to hear that we'll be in synch to start,
so the comments I added below are forward looking.

On 8/27/12 4:52 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > On Monday, August 27, 2012 3:54:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
 >
 >     Everyone: should we coordinate the releases?
 >
 >
 > I would say that every Stan release should imply a new rstan release, although it may occasionally be necessary to
 > release a new rstan without releasing a new Stan (due to CRAN policy changes, changes in packages rstan depends on, bugs
 > in R code, etc.)

I would like to stick to a

    major.minor.patch

release numbering scheme, with any change in
documented functionality implying at least a
minor version update.

I only care that Stan/RStan numberings synch
so that any RStan major.minor version will run
any major/minor-matching Stan version.

So I wouldn't have minded releasing Stan 1.0.0
when we're only up to RStan 1.0.beta.

The problem I see with Stan getting ahead of RStan
on minor version number is people reading the wrong
doc.  The install of RStan is encapsulated, so that
shouldn't cause a problem.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
J

I closed and reopened R and now it works.

So maybe this needs to be in the instructions.  After installing the package, close R and then reopen it.

Also, print() needs to be fixed:  the headers should be "mean", "se_mean", "sd", …, "n_eff", …
And in the note at the bottom of the print() output, "ESS" should be changed to "n_eff" and "samples" should be changed to "sample".

A

messages.subject: revised web site
messages.body_plain:
I revised the content of the web site with command-line
install and getting started instructions.

I'm very uncertain about what level user to aim
for in the above.

I also left the download section on the home
page and left the version numbers in the tarball
name and in (or near) the links to the tarball.

I'd be happy with just a single download link on the nav
bar, but somewhere the home page has to prominently
indicate which version we're at.  R indicates the latest
version indirectly in the "News" section after links to
"download R" and to "CRAN mirror" (which confusingly
go the same place; we skip the mirror level with
Google Code).  After selecting a mirror, you get
to another page full of links by platform, and finally
to one or more links for the platform of choice.

I like the way both Eigen and Boost arrange
their downloads.  Eigen's layout is over messy
because it's embedded in a family of apps and
the family's nav adds noise (just like Google
Code does on our Google Code page).

- Bob

messages.subject: log_post
messages.body_plain:
J

The easiest thing is to simply include log_post as one more variable to save, just throw it on the bottom of the list of variables.  The only issue is that with big models, the log posterior will be a big number in absolute value (e.g., it might be something like -24000) which will make the table look ugly.  Log_post per observation would be fine except that in general we can't really define the number of "observations."  Also it's not really the log posterior, it's really the log joint density, or maybe not even that, given that there are so many different ways to write the model.

But for now let's just go with log_post as an extra row in the table and an extra element in the plot, just the way we did deviance in r2winbugs.  Then later we can think harder about best way of doing this.

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
messages.body_plain:
Andrew:

Just a heads up that this message is one to pay attention
to.

Your and Kenny's variogram-based estimator for ESS is
defined using (k-1) in the denominator, where k is the
number of chains.  Thus we'd technically get infinite
variance estimates and thus zero ESS with a single chain.

So what Jiqiang did was just revert to the standard
estimate for a single chain instead of using the
variogram-based estimator.

The altnernative would be to not let users run Stan
with num chains = 1, which seems unduly restrictive.

I suppose a midway ground is to launch a warning to
scold the user into using three (?) or more chains.

More below on technical details of the implementation.

On 8/29/12 2:36 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I forgot to work on it.  It came to my mind that when I print the fitted object in rstan
> if I have n_chain = 1, it threw an error, I guess, due to some recent changes on
> the variance function in stan, which does not allow input of length 1.
> So I made a tiny change on the computing ess to just use the variance
> computed from one chain as the variance estimate for the parameter as we talked before.

Perfect.

Yes, I went back in and added some error checking to our
variance() function, which uses (n-1) in the denominator,
so isn't well-defined at n=1.

We could also add a second variance function that divides
by n.  I don't know how we'd call them, maybe variance()
and variance_mle()?

- Bob

messages.subject: "sample" or "samples"?
messages.body_plain:
What kind of noun is "sample" in the context
we're using it?

English has three kinds of nouns:

    singular count (e.g., student, car)
    plural count (e.g., students, cars)
    mass (e.g., water, sky)

as well as a fourth minor category of dual nouns
like "scissors" and "pants".

Which determiner (or partitive, like "a lot of")
you use depends on whether something
is a mass or count noun.

    much water / * many water
    many students / much students

When we sample from a distribution ("sample" is also
a verb), do we get a "single sample"
or "several samples"?

In the manual, I took "sample" to refer to a
complete set of parameter values derived from
a single iteration of HMC/NUTS, so a single chain
produces multiple samples, and a sampler produces
multiple samples in a run, not a single sample.

I could see this going the other way, with
a "sample" referring to a mass of samples of the
kind I talked about, being collective over one or more chains.
This would be like "we took a water sample from
this well" as opposed to "we took samples of the
chips from the production line".

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 8/29/12 5:22 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> One approach is to use the split chains we're already using for split R-hat.
 > Then we have k at least 2 for sure.

I think we followed the BDA draft for ESS, which
does NOT split the chains.  That is, it uses
unsplit var+ estimate and then whole chains
for autocovariance.

I really don't care at all how we do this,
though there's a simplicity and doc advantage
to having a single unified definition.

> In any case, we only want to report a single variance function, whatever it is we decide to do.
 > Others can always do their own post-processing if they really want.

Which "report" are you talking about?  I'm talking
about which functions are defined for use in the
Stan modeling language and which functions we define
in C++.  Right now, we have a function variance()
that divides by (N-1) and we do not have a function
that divides by N.

There's no way for a user to correct the unbiased
variance to the MLE in the case of one sample
after our version's divided by zero.  They'd have to
write a loop to calculate the MLE version of variance.

I see the same benefit in having both MLE and
unbiased versions of sample variance calcs as
having multiple parameterizations.

- Bob

of some number of samples, and being further divisible into a
subsample of a smaller number of samples).

Now all I need to know is what to call one of the
1000 thingamajigs that is in a sample of size 1000.

If our one sample of size 1000 is

    theta[1], ..., theta[1000]

where each theta[n] is a vector of parameter values,
what do I call the seventh thingamajig, theta[7]?

I was calling theta[7] a sample.

We decided to call the work done in creating a thingamajig
an "iteration."  So we might say "the sampler ran for 1000
iterations with the output from 250 of these iterations
used to form a single sample of size 250".

But I can't call theta[7] an iteration, can I?  That seems
like a type mistake.  I think of an iteration as something an
algorithm does, not something it outputs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
messages.body_plain:
Andrew -- make sure you get to the last item and
understand how integer arithmetic works in Stan and C++
(and Java and Python and every other language I know other
than BUGS, R and MATLAB).

On 8/29/12 5:55 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> I don't have a strong feeling about the ESS thing because I never run just one chain.
 > For now, I'm happy either working with the split chains or else having an "if"
 > statement so that when #chains is more than 1 it uses our formula, but when #chains=1, it splits first.

No problem.  We can change the definition.

First, I'll work through the math to make sure it works.
It seems to me like we'll just be jacking up the variance
by a fixed factor (offhand, I'm guessing 1/4) this way, but
I'll verify.

Then it requires changing not only the code, but also the Stan doc,
the RStan doc, and the Stan unit tests.  So when I or someone
else has an hour or two, we can make the changes.

 > Oh, ok.  For the variance() function in Stan we should divide by n-1.  That is standard.

It certainly matches BUGS, R and MATLAB, which is why
I coded it that way in the first place.

 > If you'd like it to also operate when n=1, the function could simply be defined as 0 when n=1.
 > (In R, var() returns NA when n=1, but I have no problem with variance() returning 0).

I'd rather throw an error.  If we return anything,
it should be +infinity.  Returning 0 seems like a recipe
for errors.

 > Then if you want the other thing, you can just compute variance*(n-1)/n and everybody will be happy.

But a special variance_mle() function would do it more
efficiently and in a way less prone to errors.

For example, the astute reader of the Stan doc would realize
that

   (n-1) / n * variance = 0

if n is an integer, because Stan follows C++ in evaluating
arithmetic expressions, which means (a) it's left associative,
making this equal to:

   ((n-1) / n) * variance

and (b) uses integer arithmetic for integers, which rounds
fractions down, so that (n-1)/n = 0.

This should probably go into the Stan-for-BUGS-users section.

Having said all this, Guido von Rossum, developer of Python,
regrets his choice to implement integer division following
C conventions:

http://python-history.blogspot.com/2009/03/problem-with-integer-division.html

- Bob

messages.subject: RStan options
messages.body_plain:
RStan looks super great.  All of the functionality we
wanted is in it and the doc's already pretty clear.

A couple of issues I brought up with Jiqiang, neither of
which is major (both have simple workarounds):

1.  Initialization in RStan doesn't take an R function to
call per chain, like R2WinBUGs, but just a list of lists for
each chain.  (As well as allowing the all-0 inits and random
inits.)

   Workaround:  run the function num_chains times and stuff into list.

2.  The data can be an environment, but there's no default.
I had thought we'd talked about taking the user's environment.

I think some others (Malecki, Ben?) were objecting to using an
environment at all.

   Workaround:  run the function with .GlobalEnv or whatever.

- Bob

I don't think stan() should be hard-coded to evaluate in .GlobalEnv . This can cause correct but unexpected behavior if stan() is being called by some other function. For example,

foo <- function(...) {
  pi <- # something not equal to 3.14ish
  posterior <- stan("my_model.stan", data = list(pi = pi))
  return(posterior)
}

If stan() evaluates in .GlobalEnv, then the pi in data{} block of my_model.stan will be 3.14ish.

What's wrong with just letting R evaluate lexically like it always does?

Ben

> foo <- function(...) {
>    pi <- # something not equal to 3.14ish
>    posterior <- stan("my_model.stan", data = list(pi = pi))
>    return(posterior)
> }
>
> If stan() evaluates in .GlobalEnv, then the pi in data{} block of my_model.stan will be 3.14ish.
>
> What's wrong with just letting R evaluate lexically like it always does?

Short answer, nothing!

This was a couple of confusions on my part.

One was the R idiom where you don't want to set
a default parameter value other than NULL,
because you may pass data in other ways.  Defaults
get confusing when there are optional arguments
that control settings (sort of like for Stan itself's
command-line control of HMC vs. NUTS through interacting
arguments).

My second confusion was about global environments.
I should've replaced ".GlobalEnv or whatever" with
"environment() or whatever".  (I only remembered the
.GlobalEnv from something in the mi interface.)

Sorry -- this is just MY lack of fluency in R.
We absolutely don't want to document the R language
as part of our own doc.

Examples of using the idioms should go in a tutorial
user's guide.  I wouldn't mind taking a whack at writing
that to force myself to learn R better.

- Bob

eval takes 60ms then each iteration could take a minute. If we're only
refreshing the screen every 20 iterations (which I believe is what
happens by default on the command line), then that means the user gets
feedback every 20 minutes, which feels a lot like hanging.

> Bad news:  in one of the chains we got the following messages during adaptation:
>
> ********************************************************************************

> Dynamic exception type: std::domain_error
> std::exception::what: Error in function stan::prob::normal_log<N4stan5agrad3varE>(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter, mu,[0]  is -inf:0, but must be finite!

>

>
> I don't know if this helps, but I will tell you that the model is not well behaved in this case.  Recall that the data in the 8-schools are slightly under dispersed, i.e. the best estimate of tau from the data is actually negative.  If you replicate 100 times, you basically get a dataset that's not consistent with the model.  Given the constraints, tau really really wants to be zero.  And when I re-fit using fake data simulated from the model, everything worked just fine.
>

Nothing is stopping us from changing the names, but to me, iter, warmup, and thin make as much sense as n_iter, n_warmup, and n_thin. I think anyone who has done any MCMC before would expect there to be an positive integer argument for the iterations and the thinning interval. But warmup is more difficult because it is nonstandard. I could see an experienced MCMC user thinking that warmup might be binary or something but making the connection that n_warmup was supposed to be a positive integer.

Ben

messages.subject: stan vs. lmer scalability
messages.body_plain:
Hey, just to let you know, I programmed up a simple hierarchical logistic regression with 10,000 data points, 150 groups, and 10 unmodeled predictors (so that the glmer model was bglmer (y ~ X + (1|group), family=binomial(link="logit"))).

bglmer (essentially same as glmer) takes 2 seconds.

stan (4 chains for 100 iterations each, not really enough but it's reasonable) takes 2 minutes and 15 seconds. (not counting compilation time)

But once bernoulli is vectorized this should help a lot, right?

I'm not saying that Stan needs to "beat" glmer, it's just an interesting speed comparison.  We're thinking of putting in Stan as an option for mrp because it can be important to have a sense of uncertainty in the estimated parameters.  Really, 2 minutes for the occasional hierarchical model run is ok, but I'm looking forward to speed improvements from the vectorization.

Convergence is fine.  It's fun to run Nuts with a problem that's this slow:  on the screen you can see that some iterations take much longer than others.  It's clear that L is a random variable.

A

messages.body_plain:
Here's a message originally from goodwin, who I just
gave posting priveleges.

I'll have to look up  the "DE" method by Vrugt and Braak
(with names like those, I'm expecting big things).

That must be one hairy model if you can only do 100K
gradient calcs/hour!

More on the content later.  I'm still trying to catch
up with our initial release issues.

And thanks for posting.

- Bob

----------

I have just become a member of stan dev list, and have been looking through messages. I have some comments/questions,
and wondered if I could have posting privileges or if there was some other suitable means of communication.

Let me explain a bit - I am developing commercial software for engineering design and Bayesian uncertainty forecasting.
This involves creating a proxy/surrogate/kriging model of a large engineering simulation package, and then applying MCMC
to determine probabilistic forecasts. I have been doing this for over ten years, but am currently upgrading my MCMC
methods. NUTS seemed to fit the bill very nicely, until I started applying it to my problem this week!

I am not in academia, but in business, but I have been working on optimisation techniques for a long time.

My likelihood function is very complex, with multiple minima and lots of curved narrow valleys. I have up to 400
parameters, but normally about 50. Derivatives are available.

I have implemented basic RW, NUTS, HMCMC, DE (Vrugt and Braak) and parallel tempering (PT), and have implemented various
combinations (e.g. DE with PT). My code is fully integrated so it is very easy to switch methods, or use different
methods at different steps, or combine methods.

The goal is a software product which is completely automatic, no user tuning of parameters, the user does not even know
MCMC is being implemented. hence the attraction of NUTS. There is a practical limit on how long a user will wait - an
hour is about the maximum. This means in practice about 100,000 function/derivative calculations.

I have converted Matlab NUTS and DE code to Java.

My current findings are that NUTS is very good on nice smooth functions with a single mode, but can fail badly on more
complex functions. In contrast, DE seems to cope well with multiple modes and complex functions.

Now, the kinds of discussions I would like to have with your colleagues are ways of improving NUTS. I am not interested
in the STAN infrastructure, just the core algorithm. They fall into several categories:

1. Simple changes.

Often the step size is small and the number of leap frogs becomes large. The step size keeps on falling because it is
difficult to find better points. The algorithm seems to easily get stuck in local minima. I know there are better points
because the espilon estimation found them, but the leap frogs cannot. Stan uses a variation on epsilon, and I am
currently trying a gamma distribution on epsilon. However, Stan seems to do this when not in burn in phase, which seems
strange as I have problems within burn in.

I am also allowing a re estimation of epsilon if the limit on the max number of depths is reached. I redo the initial
epsilon estimation.  This is a bit similar to DE where the step length is sometimes set to 1.0 to allow jumps to
alternative modes.

My epsilon estimation takes the average of 10 trials, because of the complex curvature.

An obvious improvement would be to first find a good starting point - this is my default - but I really want a method
which is robust enough to handle any starting point, and explore the space fully.

2. Integration with DE.

Because DE and NUTS seems to complement each other, it would be nice to have a method which combines them. For example,
run parallel chains, one of them NUTS the others DE. For the NUTS chain, it may be possible to use a DE approach to set
the momentum, instead of doing a Gaussian. I need to check how this would work, but it would ameliorate the problem of
steps which keep hiting high mountains. The DE approach is self adapting in that the points lie along valleys so
differences are also along valleys.

3. Integration with PT.

I have tried PT with DE, and it is useful, but I fear PT with NUTS would be too time consuming.  Because the NUTS chain
is much more expensive, because of the multiple leap frogs, it may be useful to have other DE chains which include PT
and this will not affect performance too much.

4. Better Hessian/mass matrix.

A diagonal mass matrix is no use to me, but recent studies using BFGS and/or Reimann manifold may be  beneficial. They
may not,  however, help the multi mode issue. I have tried NUTS with a simple highly correlated multivariate gaussian
distribution with an exact weight matrix, and the efficiency improves drastically.

Are these kinds of discussions suitable for the mailing list? A lot of mailing list discussions are around more basic
software issues, rather than the algorithm itself.

------------------------

messages.body_plain:
DE is a very nice method.

You can call me Nigel.

My model is a kriging/surrogate/proxy/radial basis function/Guassian process model.

In fact in the example I have been using, there are about 300 models, and the overall likelihood calculates the likelihood for each individual model.

Each individual model is based on about 600 big engineering simulation runs (which can each take 24 hours in some cases).

I use Matern correlation functions which take some time, and calculating the derivatives was fun.

So for the overall likelihood function calculation I do about 300 Cholesky solves with a 600 x 600 triangular factor. The derivative calculation takes about the same time as a function evaluation.

I do it all in heavily multi threaded Java code.

Re NUTS - I did changes to the epsilon as mentioned below, and it definitely improves things. Giving the epsilon a jolt if it gets stuck at small values help a lot. The gamma distribution may also help. Being in commerce, I don't do days and days of testing, I use my instincts a lot.

Next stage I think will be to run parallel DE chains and do some cross fertilisation a la tempering.

BTW, I find that out of the box it takes of the order of 1000 leap frog steps per iteration, so there is plenty of scope for using an approximate hessian. Using the Hessian will also make it less sensitive to the size of the momentum gaussian distribution, which is very critical.

The BFGS paper is not as well known but is also very nice work - Zhang and Sutton.

> to determine probabilistic forecasts. I have been doing this for over ten years, but am currently upgrading my MCMC

>
> methods at different steps, or combine methods.
>
>
>
> The goal is a software product which is completely automatic, no user tuning of parameters, the user does not even know
>
> MCMC is being implemented. hence the attraction of NUTS. There is a practical limit on how long a user will wait - an
>
> hour is about the maximum. This means in practice about 100,000 function/derivative calculations.
>
>
>
> I have converted Matlab NUTS and DE code to Java.
>
>
>
> My current findings are that NUTS is very good on nice smooth functions with a single mode, but can fail badly on more
>
> complex functions. In contrast, DE seems to cope well with multiple modes and complex functions.
>
>
>

>
> in the STAN infrastructure, just the core algorithm. They fall into several categories:
>
>
>
> 1. Simple changes.
>
>
>
> Often the step size is small and the number of leap frogs becomes large. The step size keeps on falling because it is
>
> difficult to find better points. The algorithm seems to easily get stuck in local minima. I know there are better points
>
> because the espilon estimation found them, but the leap frogs cannot. Stan uses a variation on epsilon, and I am
>
> currently trying a gamma distribution on epsilon. However, Stan seems to do this when not in burn in phase, which seems
>
> strange as I have problems within burn in.
>
>
>
> I am also allowing a re estimation of epsilon if the limit on the max number of depths is reached. I redo the initial
>
> epsilon estimation.  This is a bit similar to DE where the step length is sometimes set to 1.0 to allow jumps to
>
> alternative modes.
>
>
>
> My epsilon estimation takes the average of 10 trials, because of the complex curvature.
>
>
>
> An obvious improvement would be to first find a good starting point - this is my default - but I really want a method
>
> which is robust enough to handle any starting point, and explore the space fully.
>
>
>
> 2. Integration with DE.
>
>
>
> Because DE and NUTS seems to complement each other, it would be nice to have a method which combines them. For example,
>
> run parallel chains, one of them NUTS the others DE. For the NUTS chain, it may be possible to use a DE approach to set
>
> the momentum, instead of doing a Gaussian. I need to check how this would work, but it would ameliorate the problem of
>
> steps which keep hiting high mountains. The DE approach is self adapting in that the points lie along valleys so
>
> differences are also along valleys.
>
>
>
> 3. Integration with PT.
>
>
>
> I have tried PT with DE, and it is useful, but I fear PT with NUTS would be too time consuming.  Because the NUTS chain
>
> is much more expensive, because of the multiple leap frogs, it may be useful to have other DE chains which include PT
>
> and this will not affect performance too much.
>
>
>
> 4. Better Hessian/mass matrix.
>
>
>
> A diagonal mass matrix is no use to me, but recent studies using BFGS and/or Reimann manifold may be  beneficial. They
>
> may not,  however, help the multi mode issue. I have tried NUTS with a simple highly correlated multivariate gaussian
>
> distribution with an exact weight matrix, and the efficiency improves drastically.
>
>
>
> Are these kinds of discussions suitable for the mailing list? A lot of mailing list discussions are around more basic
>
> software issues, rather than the algorithm itself.
>
>
>
> ------------------------

messages.body_plain:
It is metropolis, but the step is based on difference between samples in other chains, so as the chains mature and samples lie along paths, the new points also lie on those paths. Also, if there are multiple modes, sometimes the sample difference means you can jump across modes. So it automatically self adapts without any heavy matrix arithmetic. If all the chains converge to the same point, the steps all adapt and get smaller (in optimisation mode).

It can be applied to discrete parameters, although I haven;t tried this yet - I will need the capability in the near future (i.e. next week).

The main issue is that the basic approach needs 2 x N chains, but more recent work has helped. As I sometimes have 400 parameters, this is an issue. Even with 16 parameters (which is for me on the very small side), 32 chains is quite a lot. I tend to use 8 chains, it used to be so that each chain can be on a separate CPU core, but I am doing it differently now and 8 just seems a sensible number.

A lot of the ideas come from the differential evolution method in heuristic optimisation, which I have used a lot and found very useful (much better than the 'conventional' GA operators). It works, but nobody knows why!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nigel,

I'll try to respond to some of these questions.

To clarify, Stan adapts the step size epsilon during burn-in, but not
afterwards, since adapting MCMC parameters results in a
non-time-homogeneous Markov chain which will have the wrong stationary
distribution. (I.e., you'll get samples from a distribution besides
the target posterior.) There is an option to jiggle the step size, but
the danger of doing this with NUTS is that if you use too small of a
step size then you'll wind up with a very long (and expensive)
trajectory.

NUTS tries to find the largest step size that doesn't lead to
unacceptably inaccurate simulations. The goal is to produce results
that are both as fast as possible and unlikely to produce incorrect
results—a problem with using a step size that's too large is that you
may wind up never visiting certain parts of the parameter space even
if they have a decent amount of posterior mass.

Ultimately, it's very difficult to evaluate the performance of an MCMC
algorithm on a multimodal posterior. The way I think about it is that
(a) sampling is harder than optimization (b) finding global optima is
intractable for multimodal objective functions so (c) sampling from
multimodal posteriors is intractable. So in the typical case you're
unlikely to ever get even a single "effectively independent" sample
from a multimodal distribution, since to do that you'd basically have
to be able to show that you've given each isolated mode its due
consideration.

For many practical problems, it's nonetheless useful to get a few
samples (or even one sample) from a single reasonably high-mass mode.
Even if that's a terrible summary of the posterior, it can still be a
useful result. If that's all you need, then I'd argue that you don't
actually need to use an MCMC algorithm that satisfies detailed balance
and is guaranteed to generate samples from the true posterior. Lifting
the detailed balance restriction dramatically increases the world of
algorithmic choices you can make.

Having said all that, there's certainly still plenty of room to make
NUTS better while still satisfying detailed balance! I'm not very
familiar with DE, but it's probably worth looking into. My
understanding is that it generates proposals roughly in the direction
of the vectors between points in parallel chains, an idea that's quite
closely related to Zhang and Sutton's BFGS HMC algorithm. A limitation
of these methods is that they aren't able to do any local
adaptation—if you've got a bunch of chains in different isolated
modes, then it seems likely that you're not going to get information
from chains 1 and 2 them that's relevant to the mode that chain 3 is
in. My guess is that these sorts of approaches are probably not much
more useful than using a good fixed linear preconditioner matrix
(equivalent to using a fixed covariance matrix for the momentum
distribution). But it's nice that they satisfy detailed balance and
don't require O(N^2) computation/storage.

Riemannian Manifold HMC (using the Fisher metric of Girolami and
Calderhead) is able to do local adaptation, but requires 1. a
log-concave prior (which rules out most hierarchical models) 2. the
ability to compute the derivative of the metric, which involves
computing third derivatives of the log-prior and 3. solving an N-by-N
system of equations for each step. A version of RMHMC/RMNUTS that
didn't suffer from these restrictions but still used local information
would be great, and is something I and others are actively looking at.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
1.  I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.

2.  Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).

But now I have mixed feelings.  Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.

One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-.  Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.

I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both.  That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
foo1 <- foo2
is correct, then
foo1 ~ foo2
is incorrect.  And vice-versa.  So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information.  That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok.  In any case, I'm pretty sure that when I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa.  It's just hard to keep straight.

A

On Fri, Aug 31, 2012 at 5:12 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> 1.  I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.

Thinking about it more, I would also propose normal_random to be
consistent with normal_log, normal_cdf etc.

>
> 2.  Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).
>
> But now I have mixed feelings.  Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.
>
> One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-.  Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.
>
> I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both.  That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
> foo1 <- foo2
> is correct, then
> foo1 ~ foo2
> is incorrect.  And vice-versa.  So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information.  That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok.  In any case, I'm pretty sure that when I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa.  It's just hard to keep straight.

In the model block

foo1 <- foo2(a,b)

is not the same as

foo1 ~ foo2(a,b)

The first means assignment of a value (i.e., in C++ foo1 = foo2(a,b);)
while the second declares something as being distributed according to
a distribution.  The second gets translated into:

lp__ += foo2_log(foo1,a,b);

I prefer overloading ~ because it has an intuitive match to a commonly
used notation.  In the generated quantities block the second statement
would become something like:

random_normal(foo1,a,b);

Note that this does imply a restricted statement syntax for the LHS of
a ~ in the generated quantities block.  I suppose that's the one
advantage of using <- in generated quantities because that rule would
be consistent.

Cheers,
Marcus
